He will recall this post-coming-out phase of his life as the Year of Damp Feet, spent forever popping into the shower to rinse off his dick and stomach.

It was four sentences. He’d created a listserv for the recipients: family, friends, and coworkers. After he closed his eyes, downed two shots of vodka, and hit “send,” he knew what was going to come to him. His colleagues would whisper about his deviant sexual activity; inevitably, he’d get kicked out on the street with his box of desk supplies (a dried-up fern and a hand gripper). Not to mention his poor mother—her wracking sobs, her inevitable refusal to speak to him, the prodigal son, ever again. After sending, he paced around the room, drank four additional shots, and cried in the bathroom. By the time that he’d finished the anxious rigamarole, a few replies had come in, and the reality became obvious: he’d been received with open-arms and heart emojis. His boss, Greg, replied: “Great for you, bud.” On the phone, his parents told him that they still loved him; in fact, they’d thought he might’ve been—well, not heterosexual. In the days after he’d sent the email, he didn’t feel compelled to download any apps or sit at a stool in the gay bar down the street. A part of him wished for adversity, or at least the accompanying opportunity to rise above it, but he was left with an understanding that nothing had changed, that declaration didn’t always inspire action. Instead, he spent the rest of the post-coming-out year taking his lunch to-go and eating at his desk, lifting dumbbells in front of “Housewives of SLC,” and referring to it as “The Year of Damp Feet,” meaning he went straight from the shower to the bed without toweling off.

written_by_MFA011.Original: It takes Kant a year to write the one-paragraph mass email, another three weeks to compile the Coming Out mailing list of friends, family, and colleagues, and three bourbons to actually send it. For his entire life he has so grotesquely imagined the consequences of public exposure that he’s only recently, at thirty-one, stopped hedging to himself that he is bi or “flexible.” He pictures his mother saying she never wants to speak to him again; he imagines dying alone in an unheated tenement, though he knows this is unlikely to happen to a video-game asset designer with two degrees. Part of him had believed that as long as his proclivities resided only in his head, and sometimes on his computer, they didn’t “count.” Now everyone will know; his sexuality will exist as an open fact. After sending the email, he turns off his phone and spends the night vomiting from stress.But the response is unanimously supportive. His friends reply with the visible spectrum of heart emojis. His coworkers politely underreact (“Oh neat! Psyched for you”). Kant’s parents are not thrilled exactly—they wish he’d called them first, though he couldn’t fathom doing this twice—yet they are neither disapproving nor surprised. The recent legalization of gay marriage probably helped; mainly his parents want to know whether he still plans on having kids, and he says yes, just to give them something.Perversely he sort of wishes the response had been more dramatic and adverse, to give him something to overcome, forcing growth in the process, though he knows he doesn’t really want that. But having tailored his life to compensate for its lack of relationships, there’s nothing compelling him to act on his new freedom, and instead he’s masturbating more than ever. He will recall this post-coming-out phase of his life as the Year of Damp Feet, spent forever popping into the shower to rinse off his dick and stomach.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: Kant writes the email and spends a long time editing it, making minor changes to the wording only to change them back to exactly what he’d written before. He thinks about his upbringing and all the years that this information has weighed on him: the kids in middle school who tackled him in the locker room and forced him to eat dog shit, the fact that he couldn’t even admit to himself that he wanted to watch gay porn until he was twenty-five. Paralyzed, still editing, he imagines his mother’s disgust upon reading the email, imagining her 31-year-old son doing exactly what he’d done for the better part of the last two decades: that is, fanatasizing about some buff, hairy dude he saw online. He imagines himself dying alone, ostracized from anyone who might love him, the nerves in his dick beginning to desensitize from too much dry-hand masturbation. When he sends the email, though, the responses are surprisingly anticlimactic. He gets a few heart emojis from friends; some coworkers reply with “nice,” and “good for you!” Even his parents are mostly supportive, though his mom expresses some mild annoyance that he hadn’t called first to warn them. Kant feels a mixture of intense relief, combined with an unpleasant sense of disappointment that he finds difficult to face. Where was the fallout, the dramatic messages and cut-off relationships from family members? Why didn’t anyone care? He had once imagined his post-coming out life as a time of transformation, a new life like a beautiful patterned carpet rolling out before him, but instead he finds himself stuck in the exact same state of stasis that emboldened him to write the email in the first place. He begins to call this period his “Year of Damp Feet,” as his feet are constantly sweaty despite the fact that he rarely moves them from beneath his computer desk.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: What happened was—well, a lot happened. It took him a full year of latent DELAYED_MAIL exponential backoff before he managed to send a taut, defensive email to a BCC list of family, friends, and coworkers, coming up with some bullshit Aristotelian lie about fairness and specifically that it's totally unfair to ever be in the closet at all. He sent it out in the early morning hours of his 31st birthday, then paced up and down his hallway imagining worst-case replies: "You're dead to me"; "My poor boy, where did we go wrong"; "The priest has offered to counsel you"; "It sounds like you're legitimizing pederasty" . . . all cathected to a schizo runway reel of potential future selves: talented softcore pornographer with an 80-inch TV crashed out depressed on a couch with his own green-tinted face reflected in the screen; or candle-hoarding Toronto shut-in in a stuffed-animal bramble; or solitary defiant hedonist having foolish condomless sex and convicted of murder based on DNA evidence. He finally counted 18 breaths and, to delay longer, opened up a new doc and composed the marriage proposal he'd send to the first man to make him cum without dildos or videos. written_by_MFA024.Excerpt2: Kant wrote thirty versions of his coming-out email over the course of ten months. Though he knew better, he couldn’t keep from anticipating and meticulously addressing, in the email itself, the various surprised, dismissive, or condemnatory responses of his friends and family, to the point where the email was less an act of claiming his own reality than a bullish bracing of himself against an incoming bilgewater tide of others’ realities. He clicked send. Feeling noble, self-satisfied, and above all ready, he camped at his laptop with an energy drink and spammed refresh. A couple hours later, an email from his father sent a spike of fear into his chest: he was about to be disowned. But while not exactly celebratory, the message indicated uncomplicated respect and acceptance. An email from an old college friend came in next, composed only of emojis. Where was their disgust? Their bitterness and disdain? The underwhelm was itself an overwhelm: he felt ridiculous, mocked by precisely an absence of mockery. Coming out should feel like something, shouldn’t it? He considered, by way of analogy, his own naïve expectation every birthday that he might experience an inner shift adequate to the day’s significance, a radiance, a spiritual lift, some kind of internal popping sound at least—I’m twenty-nine!—and instead met again and again just another day. Wasn’t this exactly how all life’s big events felt? A non-feeling? Supportive replies rolled in, and each refused to move the plot of his life forward. He’d imagined that this one symbolic action would release something huge and wild in him, that he’d start going on dates, he’d kiss the real flesh of a real guy; but months later he was still eating the same Cheez-Its and masturbating to the same porn, only now he didn’t even bother to clean up after himself. What he’d imagined calling The Year of Freedom had become The Year of Damp Feet.

written_by_MFA010.Original: For Christmas, my father bought me a sweater and a shirt, but later he gave me an envelope containing ten hundred-dollar bills. “You will need it for this and that,” he said when I told him it was too much. My father had also arranged to go to Disney World for five days; this, along with the toys under the tree, was his present to the girls. “You are welcome to join us,” my father said when he announced this news on Christmas morning, but I said no, making up something about there being a winter session at Swarthmore. My father did not try to persuade me. But Rupa and Piu were devastated. “Why don’t you want to come?” they kept asking, all the more bewildered when they discovered that I had never been to Disney World. I sensed that they needed me, as I needed them, to mask the growing, incontrovertible fact that Chitra and my father now formed a couple. My presence was proof that my mother had once existed, just as they represented the physical legacy of their dead father. “Won’t you be lonely by yourself?” Chitra asked me more than once. At the same time, I gathered that she, like my father, was relieved to hear my plans. I had no plans, of course, other than to be in the house alone.
written_by_MFA010.Excerpt1: That year, at Christmas, my father gave me three crisp hundred-dollar bills instead of a gift. He invited me to join him and Chitra and Rupa and Piu at Disney World, where they were planning to spend part of the girls' winter vacation. I told him I couldn't go because school started up again the day after New Year's, but I didn't tell him that I checked the calendar first and realized that we would be back in plenty of time. To make up for it, I bought my half sisters ridiculously expensive presents—a record player for Rupa and a camera for Piu. Rupa cried when I told her I wasn't going to Disney World, which was where the record player and camera would be put to use. Piu put her arms around me. "I don't understand you, Didi," she said, still in her small, high voice. "What did we do wrong that makes you not want to go?" The truth was that in my eyes they had done nothing wrong, whereas I was punished by their mere existence. But I was still convinced that it was up to me to honor my mother's memory, just as they instinctively honored the man who was their father but not really mine. Still, I sensed that Chitra was relieved by my decision, and, by extension, so was my father.
written_by_MFA010.Excerpt2: I was home during winter. On Christmas morning, my father entered my room with a thin, white envelope in hand. Inside, there were ten twenty-dollar notes, totalling a sum of two hundred dollars, the most generous amount I had ever received from my father. I thanked him profusely, but it seemed like a prologue to the real question my father wanted to ask me. He invited me to Disney World, where he was planning to take Chitra, his new wife, and my two half-sisters, Rupa and Piu, during spring break. But I felt distant from his new family, like a string being pulled from both ends. I fabricated some excuse about having to be on-campus during that time since I was a Resident Assistant, and declined his invitation. Later that week, as we sat on the floor circled around the Christmas tree in our living room, Rupa and Piu expressed their disappointment. They could not understand why I would not want to join them in Disney World. "It's Disney World," they exclaimed. But I kept thinking of my late mother, and everything I owed her. I felt a responsibility to hold back, to stay with her memory, as if her place in our family was still untouched and unoccupied, in the same way that Rupa and Piu symbolized and remained committed to their father’s legacy. Besides, I felt, with a strange ease, that Chitra and my father, too, were relieved by my decision to leave the four of them alone to enjoy their holiday.

written_by_MFA032.Original: For Christmas, my father bought me a sweater and a shirt, but later he gave me an envelope containing ten hundred-dollar bills. “You will need it for this and that,” he said when I told him it was too much. My father had also arranged to go to Disney World for five days; this, along with the toys under the tree, was his present to the girls. “You are welcome to join us,” my father said when he announced this news on Christmas morning, but I said no, making up something about there being a winter session at Swarthmore. My father did not try to persuade me. But Rupa and Piu were devastated. “Why don’t you want to come?” they kept asking, all the more bewildered when they discovered that I had never been to Disney World. I sensed that they needed me, as I needed them, to mask the growing, incontrovertible fact that Chitra and my father now formed a couple. My presence was proof that my mother had once existed, just as they represented the physical legacy of their dead father. “Won’t you be lonely by yourself?” Chitra asked me more than once. At the same time, I gathered that she, like my father, was relieved to hear my plans. I had no plans, of course, other than to be in the house alone.

He invited me to join him and Chitra and Rupa and Piu at Disney World, where they were planning to spend part of the girls' winter vacation. I told him I couldn't go because school started up again the day after New Year's, but I didn't tell him that I checked the calendar first and realized that we would be back in plenty of time. To make up for it, I bought my half sisters ridiculously expensive presents—a record player for Rupa and a camera for Piu. Rupa cried when I told her I wasn't going to Disney World, which was where the record player and camera would be put to use. Piu put her arms around me. "I don't understand you, Didi," she said, still in her small, high voice. "What did we do wrong that makes you not want to go?" The truth was that in my eyes they had done nothing wrong, whereas I was punished by their mere existence. But I was still convinced that it was up to me to honor my mother's memory, just as they instinctively honored the man who was their father but not really mine. Still, I sensed that Chitra was relieved by my decision, and, by extension, so was my father.
written_by_MFA032.Excerpt2: Neither were presents he could have wrapped, he said, in a tone at once defensive and apologetic. “You didn’t have to get me anything,” I said. First, he conjured a creased envelope from his shirt pocket, inside which were two crisp hundred-dollar bills, but no note, no card. The invitation to Disney World came next, in that same laconic way. Unlike the cash, it was entirely intangible. There’s no pressure.” Meanwhile, Rupa bounded toward me and Piu followed, talking over each other as they hammered out the details.I was still holding the envelope when it struck me that the tree in their living room was new-—a real Douglas Fir, not the artificial tree, which had infused the winters of my own youth, which my mother decorated with the ornaments I made at preschool. “I would love to,” I said, looking at my father, whose eyes remained elsewhere, “but classes are starting up so soon, and with the teaching load this semester… I should work.” The girls crumpled immediately. “But, but, but why?” My father simply nodded his head gravely, as if we had come to a painful, but just, compromise. “I understand,” he said, “I understand.”

written_by_MFA029.Original: I went to a cooking specialty store and bought a kitchen timer and a huge aluminum pot, big enough to bathe a German shepherd in, then went around to all the supermarkets that catered to foreigners, gathering an assortment of odd-sounding spices. I picked up a pasta cookbook at the bookstore, and bought tomatoes by the dozen. I purchased every brand of spaghetti I could lay my hands on, simmered every sauce known to man. Fine particles of garlic, onion, and olive oil swirled in the air, forming a harmonious cloud that penetrated every corner of my tiny apartment, permeating the floor and the ceiling and the walls, my clothes, my books, my records, my tennis racquet, my bundles of old letters. It was a fragrance one might have smelled on ancient Roman aqueducts.This is a story from the Year of Spaghetti, 1971 A.D.As a rule, I cooked spaghetti, and ate it, by myself. I was convinced that spaghetti was a dish best enjoyed alone. I can’t really explain why I felt that way, but there it is.I always drank tea with my spaghetti and ate a simple lettuce-and-cucumber salad. I’d make sure I had plenty of both. I laid everything out neatly on the table and enjoyed a leisurely meal, glancing at the paper as I ate. From Sunday to Saturday, one Spaghetti Day followed another. And each new Sunday started a brand-new Spaghetti Week
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: During that time I was much consumed by spaghetti. The process of cooking it was satisfying, but the idea of perfecting it was addictive. Like any dedicated student, I gathered the necessary equipment. I purchased a large pot and a kitchen timer from the specialty store across town and stocked up on spices, tomatoes, and all the pastas under the sun. The supermarket I bought the ingredients from was a place that catered to foreigners, but no one seemed to question my presence there. In a way, spaghetti and I were still strangers to each other. Back in my apartment, the experimenting began. What I lacked in formal training I had to make up for in creativity. I cooked feverishly. The smell of garlic was in my hair; the smell of onion was in the carpet; the smell of olive oil was in the wallpaper. Spaghetti sauce consumed me and the place I called home. It even spilled into my dreams. It was very important that I only ate spaghetti alone. It’s the kind of dish that insists on solitude. Before I knew it, I was following a new routine. Spaghetti was the centerpiece of every meal—balanced out, of course, by tea and a simple salad. My blissful Spaghetti Days stretched on and on from Sunday to Sunday. If there was an end in sight, I didn’t want to see it.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: Of course I didn’t think of it as cooking. In my mind it was just boiling spaghetti. I’d pull on my windbreaker and canvas sneakers, hop on my old bike and pedal to the neighborhood specialty store and gather the tools and ingredients I’d need to make spaghetti. A big pot, a thousand-yen strainer, two plates, a kitchen timer, a quart of olive oil, a head of garlic, and two onions. Supermarkets that catered to foreigners sold spaghetti. Displayed on their shelves were about ten brands in packages of every imaginable color. I bought a different brand and a small tin of spices each week. The old wooden creel hung from the handlebar would rattle and groan under the load on the way home. It just so happened that I had an old roasted-coffee mill in the cabinet under the sink that I could adjust to make minced garlic. Then I filled the place with the tantalizing aroma of garlic, onion, and olive oil, and I’d cook spaghetti sauce by the gallon and bend my head over each day’s spaghetti. Alone, at the kitchen table, no TV, no radio. Spaghetti was the only thing I could think of that was perfect for a meal eaten alone. Each and every time I’d prepare one extra little salad and one extra pot of tea…and each and every time my spaghetti would be submerged, swallowed up. Completely. So it was Spaghetti Days, from Sunday to Sunday.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: Again these are both close, but I think E1 is a bit closer. The original uses hyperbolic language for effect – “ big enough to bathe a German shepherd in”; “I purchased every brand of spaghetti I could lay my hands on, simmered every sauce known to man”; “penetrated every corner” – and E1 does this as well: “the kind of dish that insists on solitude”; “ Spaghetti sauce consumed me and the place I called home. It even spilled into my dreams.”; “ If there was an end in sight, I didn’t want to see it.”. The language is not exactly the same, but the hyperbolic effect is similar. Compare this to E2: “I bought a different brand and a small tin of spices each week” for example, is not nearly as hyperbolic as “every brand I could lay my hands on” or “spaghetti sauce consumed me”.

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: I call them the Spaghetti Days (they lasted an entire week but the singular week standing alone bothers me). On my way home from work, I’d pass the kitchen utility store where, in the shop window, there sat a stack of metal pots. I wanted the bottom one, the one shining against the rain the day I stepped through the shop door. Buying an empty pot felt wrong—too spacious—so I also bought an egg timer. But it rattled hollow around the pot. I kept walking until I reached the foreign supermarket with its crates of imported tomatoes under the awning. I put some tomatoes in that pot along with white onions, garlic, oregano, a green glass bottle of olive oil, and boxes and boxes of dry spaghetti. This, for me, was the start of a deep ritual. Steam from the boiling water fogged my kitchen window as I imagined having guests share my tea and salad. They’d comment on the nuance in smells and praise my subtle changes with the sauce and spices. But an audience would have been too much, too cramped and restricting. Spaghetti was best enjoyed alone. And being alone, there were always leftovers I’d scoop into a plastic container. At the end of the week, when it couldn’t fit any more spaghetti, I emptied all of it into the trash. No matter how hard I scrubbed the container, I couldn’t get the red stains out. I threw out the container too.

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: I call them the Spaghetti Days (they lasted an entire week but the singular week standing alone bothers me). But it rattled hollow around the pot. I kept walking until I reached the foreign supermarket with its crates of imported tomatoes under the awning. I put some tomatoes in that pot along with white onions, garlic, oregano, a green glass bottle of olive oil, and boxes and boxes of dry spaghetti. This, for me, was the start of a deep ritual. Steam from the boiling water fogged my kitchen window as I imagined having guests share my tea and salad. written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: Around seven years ago now I would go down to the Italian Market, weekends, to stock up on what I soon deemed the essentials: oregano, bay leaves, fennel seeds, butter, lemon. written_by_MFA012.Original: The day that Junior fell down began like any other day: the explosion of heat rippling the air, the trumpeting sunlight, the traffic’s tidal surges, the prayer chants in the distance, the cheap film music rising from the floor below, the loud pelvic thrusts of an 'item number' dancing across a neighbor’s TV, a child’s cry, a mother’s rebuke, unexplained laughter, scarlet expectorations, bicycles, the newly plaited hair of schoolgirls, the smell of strong sweet coffee, a green wing flashing in a tree. Senior and Junior, two very old men, opened their eyes in their bedrooms on the fourth floor of a sea-green building on a leafy lane, just out of sight of Elliot’s Beach, where, that evening, the young would congregate, as they always did, to perform the rites of youth, not far from the village of the fisherfolk, who had no time for such frivolity. The poor were puritans by night and day. As for the old, they had rites of their own and did not need to wait for evening. With the sun stabbing at them through their window blinds, the two old men struggled to their feet and lurched out onto their adjacent verandas, emerging at almost the same moment, like characters in an ancient tale, trapped in fateful coincidences, unable to escape the consequences of chance.
written_by_MFA012.Excerpt1: The day heated up and we heard the prayer bells in the temples, the bhangra beats from the music trucks plying their enthusiastic trade, the untuneful crying of children. It was time for coffee, and coffee, and coffee yet again, and lemon rice garnished with fried cashews, and all the other wondrous concoctions on offer in Madras. The two old men on the fourth floor of their sea-green building were released from their rooms by the day off like ships slipping their moorings, but they were rusty and they didn't go very far. Their names were blazoned across mailboxes and doorbells. Crowds of the young were descending upon Elliot's Beach, young men in cricket gear, young women deep in laughter and high fragrance, lovers hating their separation; and bikes, bikes, bikes. The sea was a water lily, the young people there were bees. Just a few short years ago Senior and Junior would have been down there too, scampering with the best, but now they had their own slow dance. They woke up just before noon and put on their two-day-old clothes. As if, by some mysterious machinery of fate, the timing wheels within their thickening, aging frames had been perfectly synchronized, they stepped out onto their verandahs at almost the same precise second and stood looking out into the world.
written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: And so the day passed. In the center of the city, the maghrib rang out its ancient melody, warring with the Tamil music lilting out of the speakers of a passing rickshaw—the ocean swell of strings, the buoyant theme of an old Hollywood film. The aroma of filter coffee boiled up from the terraces of the cafes, which were filled with tourists from Tuscany, Madrid, Tyrol. In other neighborhoods, children rendezvoused with their peers in shady alleyways, holding tense diplomatic summits over their games of tag. The heat lingered over the city like a sinister spirit cavalry, a battalion of jinns casting spells over Elliot’s Beach; over the twin harbors and colonial promenade; over the government center and the inland districts; and back out again to one sea-green apartment building, on the fourth floor of which there were two empty verandahs. In the corresponding room, two men simultaneously awakened from their afternoon naps and stepped out onto these verandahs, which it should be said were no longer empty. Senior and Junior, as the men were called by their respective acquaintances, did not look at each other; nor did they watch the youth wander lazily from the streets to the promenade, passing marijuana cigarettes down the line like the world’s slowest relay team. Senior and Junior looked out at Elliot’s Beach, this strange sandy coin that had been cast away by fate.
written_by_MFA012.Reason: These two are also close, but E2 is a little closer. Like the original, both excerpts focus on a series of vivid, sensory-rich details of the area surrounding the old mens’ apartment building. But the repetition used in E1 – “...lovers hating their separation; and bikes, bikes, bikes”; “ It's time for coffee, and coffee, and coffee yet again…” – is a stylistic device that isn’t used in the original. And while the original does use metaphor, this sentence in P1: “The sea was a water lily, the young people there were bees” is more abstract than anything in the original, which tends toward easy to follow simile: “like characters in an ancient tale, trapped in fateful coincidences, unable to escape the consequences of chance.” E2 sticks more closely to this formula, for example: “ The heat lingered over the city like a sinister spirit cavalry, a battalion of jinns casting spells over Elliot’s Beach; over the twin harbors and colonial promenade;...”

Once already, in the name of goodness, he’d sullied himself with murder. Shouldn’t he at least try to kill this new, even more evil, premier? Otherwise, what had it all been about?Killing the new premier would entail killing another set of unlucky diners. For him: more panic attacks, fresh nightmares. This time, if he succeeded, he would at least take some credit. Good God, yes, he would: no more silent suffering in anonymity. Afterward, he would climb up on the hood of his red car and, addressing the people, propose a new movement that would eschew violence and rule by justice and gentleness forever. Also firmness, of course. A merciful firmness the people would instantly respect.Or he could forget the whole thing, go back to being the man he’d been before the first killing: a frightened, passive nobody.This thought made him sicker than the thought of another round of screaming and crunching.He leaped out of the still running red car, threw the garage door open, and, feeling alive and decisive, stood blinking in the morning sunlight, readying himself for his task.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: One Saturday morning he sat in a red car moldering in his dead uncle's garage, hidden from view, eating Lorna Doones and listening to traffic reports, justifying to God his intent to liquidate the present, more evil, more avaricious premier. Hadn't he already demonstrated superb moral consistency by personally garroting the former premier in the Department of Rhetoric's parking garage? Hadn't he, that evening, leapt into his own pit of blood and terror, and since paid the price in terms of panic attacks and nightmares, for the advancement of humanity? Would he now declare that brave killing a merely private matter by failing to publicly acknowledge his authorship and radicalize the masses to move on, killing each corrupt premier for years to come until, exhausted, he handed the torch to some fierce young protégé? Would he? Or would he turn coward and slink back to a pasty-gray anonymous existence, wherein he walked around guilty, not of a specific criminal act (for he still held his rationale sound and remembered the strangled look of terror on the premier's face with satisfaction), but of doing nothing overall, nothing yet memorable, in the direction of righteousness? Dear Lord, if at this late date he turned cowardly, wouldn't he hate himself worse than ever? Wouldn't he? And then he leaped out of the car.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: That Saturday morning the light was orange through the window in his uncle's garage, bouncing off against the car, making the red paint seem redder. His uncle's ghost had made an appearance in the man's dream last night, making woosh-whee-whooo sounds. There were also smears of blood and the sound of the last scream of the man he had killed. The former premier. A Nouveu Fascist, the worst kind you could be, other than a Neo-Nouveu Fascist, which was much worse. The dreams had started after the pull of the gun (the newest Bang Alert model, funny, because it was a silent gun) that caused the last scream of the Nouveu Fascist. And now, on his lap, the faded picture of the Neo-Nouveu Fascist, who could be the next target of the Bang Alert. Could be? Would be. Would be his next target. And afterwards, the masses would flock around him chanting revolution, the city burning and a new one emerging. Yes, would be. No going back to the man he was before the Bang Alert, the man who slept soundly but never did anything besides that. So what if hearing another last scream meant never getting rid of the nightmares. He kicked open the door of the car and stepped out, slinging the Bang Alert across his chest. Who knew what this next last scream might sound like.

written_by_MFA029.Original: I watched my mother. It was March, and outside, the sun glinted off the sidewalks and the icy edges of the snow. It was Saint Patrick’s Day and the nurses brought my mother a square block of green Jell-O that sat quivering on the table beside her. It was the last full day of her life, and my mother did not sleep, she did not wake. She held her eyes still and open. They were the bluest thing in the room, perhaps in all of Duluth. Bluer than the lake. They were the color of the sky on the best day of your life.My mother died fast but not all of a sudden. A slow-burning fire when flames disappear to smoke and then smoke to air. She never once closed her eyes. First they were bitter and then they were bewildered and then they changed again to something else, to a state that I have had, finally, to see as heroic. Blue, blue eyes. Daggers of blue wanting and wanting. To stay, to stay.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: It was Saint Patrick's Day, though in her room there was no evidence of that. The world outside her window was still just ice-crusted heaps of snow and muddy patches. The sunlight reflected off them and whooshed in, bursting onto her ceiling. A tray with a small bowl of wobbly green Jell-O sat on a table over her bed, uneaten. My mother's arms lay on top of the blanket, waxy and unrecognizable to me now. I sat beside her, holding her hands, kissing them. She didn't seem to register that I was there anymore, though she was not asleep. She would not allow herself to sleep. Her eyes were wide open and still wildly, unquestionably, irrepressibly blue. Bluer than the sky. Bluer than the enamel-blue tulip-shaped pot that Bruce would get in the mail a few days later. Bluer than the water I'd swum across. Her eyes were the bluest balls of fire, and throughout those three weeks they blazed at me—bitter, bewildered, desolate, honest, true—and then the last six days, as she bore down to refuse sleep, they shifted to a blue that was so quiet, so heroically faithful, so fucking insistent. Insistent upon what, I didn't know. Her will, I supposed. To live.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: My mother died on St. Patrick’s Day. There was snow outside, and sunlight glanced off the ice and back into her hospital room. A cup of green Jell-O lingered untouched on its tray. My mother was unresponsive, but not quite asleep. Her eyes were open and vivid. There was an alertness in them still, but what she was looking at, I could not say. The bright blue of her irises was like a frozen lake, contrasting the dull wash of beige and gray shrouding the room. The sky lived inside my mother. It lived inside her then, too, even as we bided time together at the very end, knowing there was only one thing left for her to do. Her fading life was a fire flickering down to smoke—it would only last as long as there was something to burn. There was bitterness too in her eyes, then bewilderment, then a stoic, quiet heroism. A commitment to her own dignity. A promise to endure this final test, no matter how unfairly it had been imposed on her. Her eyes were so blue, my mother’s eyes, a fierce blue, a frozen lake, a sheen of ice that refused to melt, even as the sun broke it apart.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: E2 is closer to the original. E1 is written in as less minimalist, taut style, bringing in imagined events outside of the present action involving other characters (“Bluer than the enamel-blue tulip-shaped pot that Bruce would get in the mail a few days later”), and ascribing motivations to the mother (“She didn't seem to register that I was there anymore, though she was not asleep. She would not allow herself to sleep.”) that make the narrative less focused. In E2, like the original, the mother’s expressions are described but the narrator doesn’t speculate on her internal emotions (E2: “ Her eyes were open and vivid. There was an alertness in them still, but what she was looking at, I could not say.” Original: “It was the last full day of her life, and my mother did not sleep, she did not wake. She held her eyes still and open.”) The descriptions are focused on present action and objects in the room, with limited comparisons to features of hte local environment, as opposed to the “enamel-blue pot” referenced in P1. (E2: “ The bright blue of her irises was like a frozen lake, contrasting the dull wash of beige and gray shrouding the room.” original: “They were the bluest thing in the room, perhaps in all of Duluth. Bluer than the lake.”)

written_by_MFA012.Excerpt1: On March 17th, the world was green, but my mother’s eyes were blue. Blue as the sky in early spring. Blue as the Joni Mitchell album. Blue as the bitterness within them, my mother’s undefeated eyes. I was losing her, on that snowy day in spring. Yet she didn’t try to sleep, she didn’t give in, she didn’t snuff out the inner fire of her. She gazed out the window, bewildered by the partiers, the people dressed for Saint Patrick’s Day. The city streets were alive with voices. Sunlight danced along the surface of the Jell-O. She didn’t eat, she just looked at it, that fucking glob of green. And when she looked away, I knew she would die. Her fire had burned away. All the years of shattered sparks and roaring flame and now she was only ashes. Twin flames burning low. I hadn’t always loved my mother in life. We had had our difficulties, that was for damn sure. But as she lay on that bed, showing the blue steel of her eyes, I knew what my mother was. She was a hero. She was a fighter. She was the strongest woman I’ve known. Her lips moved a little, and I leaned in close. Grasping for her life, she slipped away.

written_by_MFA011.Original: It was early winter, the first frost of the year. My 22-year-old mother crawled into the kitchen and boiled some water to sterilise a pair of scissors. Fumbling in her sewing box, she found some white cloth that would do for a newborn’s gown. Gripped by contractions and terribly afraid, tears started down as she plied her needle. She finished the tiny gown, found a thin quilt to use as swaddling bands, and gritted her teeth as the pain returned, quicker and more intense each time.Eventually, she gave birth. Still alone, she cut the umbilical cord. She dressed the bloodied little body in the gown she’d just made, and held the whimpering scrap in her arms. For god’s sake don’t die, she muttered in a thin voice, over and over like a mantra. After an hour had passed, the baby’s tight-sealed eyelids abruptly unseamed. As my mother’s eyes encountered those of her child, her lips twitched again. For god’s sake don’t die. Around an hour later, the baby was dead. They lay there on the kitchen floor, my mother on her side with the dead baby clutched to her chest, feeling the cold gradually leach into the flesh, sinking through to the bone. No more crying.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: It was early winter already, and once it got dark the room was piteously cold. While there was still light, my mother got up and went into the kitchen. She filled the biggest rice bowl with water, then put it on the gas burner and waited for it to come to the boil. She snipped a length of white thread from the spool in her sewing box, and gently pressed a small pair of scissors into the steaming water. When the pain became so insupportable that she could no longer stand up, she lay down in the middle of the room. Labor began at around midnight. Trembling with fear, she used a scrap of white cloth to swaddle the newborn, as thin as a rat, and tied the thread around the barely pulsating umbilical cord. Then she severed it. She held the baby to her breast and murmured, Live, please live. Go on living and become my son. She continued to murmur to herself even as its barely open eyes closed for the final time. Go on. Keep going. After that, silence. The cold from the earthen floor invaded her back. Soaked into and through her flesh. Matching her lifeless child.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: My mother once told me a story about her struggle to give birth more than forty years ago, alone in her parents’ house in Apgujeong. It was early winter. The trees were bare and the ground hard. With shaky steps, she described pacing about the kitchen while she boiled water in order to sterilize the scissors that she knew she’d need to cut the cord. With the fabric in her sewing box, she fashioned a small gown and began to wear it. During the waves of pain from her contractions, she would grip at the kitchen counter hard. Eventually after hours of this the baby came out wet and covered in a fuzzy-looking substance. Still alone, she held the newborn. Chanting a desperate plea for the little thing’s survival over and over again. But after a fleeting moment of brilliant life, her newborn child went still and died. My mother lay on the floor of the kitchen. Silently, clutching at the lifeless body of what was once vibrant inside of her. As she continued to lay there with the dead child, frozen in grief, the warmth from her body departed into the frigid floor. As though the temperature of the house were somehow reflective of her inner state.
written_by_MFA011.Reason: E1is closer to the original. Both excerpts use a clipped, terse narrative style, with major actions described in short, matter-of-fact sentences (P1: “Then she severed it.”; “After that, silence.” Original: “ Still alone, she cut the umbilical cord.” “Around an hour later, the baby was dead.”) Both excerpts leap right into the mother’s story without any framing device for the narrative, whereas E2 uses the framing device of a story told in retrospect: “My mother once told me a story about her struggle to give birth more than forty years ago, alone in her parents’ house in Apgujeong.” We can assume this is the case in the other excerpts, but the fact it is not said makes those excerpts more direct and stylistically similar. E2 also uses emotional language to describe the action: “after a fleeting moment of brilliant life”; “she continued to lay there with the dead child, frozen in grief”; whereas these emotional descriptions are absent in the other two excerpts.

Then the infant slipped away without ever uttering a cry. Mother and baby, alone; forever.

While “a statue of grief” in the penultimate sentence is an interesting metaphor, emphasizing the permanence of grief, the final sentence again feels uninspired and basic “Mother and baby, alone; forever.”

written_by_MFA008.Original: That's ridiculous, he says. I'm not going to New York without you. I wouldn't even be here if it wasn't for you.It's true, she thinks, he wouldn’t be. He would be somewhere else entirely, living a different kind of life. He would be different with women even, and his aspirations for love would be different. And Marianne herself, she would be another person completely. Would she ever have been happy? And what kind of happiness might it have been? All these years they've been like two little plants sharing the same plot of soil, growing around one another, contorting to make room, taking certain unlikely positions. But in the end she has done something for him, she’s made a new life possible, and she can always feel good about that. I'd miss you too much, he says. I’d be sick, honestly. At first. But it would get better. They sit in silence now, Marianne moving the brush methodically through her hair, feeling for knots and slowly, patiently untangling them. There's no point in being impatient anymore. You know I love you, says Connell. I'm never going to feel the same way for someone else. She nods, okay. He's telling the truth. To be honest, I don’t know what to do, he says. Say you want me to stay and I will. She closes her eyes. He probably won’t come back, she thinks. Or he will, differently. What they have now they can never have back again. But for her the pain of loneliness will be nothing to the pain that she used to feel, of being unworthy. He brought her goodness like a gift and now it belongs to her. Meanwhile his life opens out before him in all directions at once. They’ve done a lot of good for each other. Really, she thinks, really. People can really change one another.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Marianne says nothing for a time. Her arm, his arm, her leg. Maybe we could, if it’s just going to be a year, she says. Don’t think other people have gone through life without having long periods of time on their own, you know. Yes, he says. I just love you so much. I know, she says. I love you too. He nods, breathing in. Her large dark eyes are like openings to something. Without you I would be nothing, he says. I would just be a shadow walking around the town. I saw you, I really saw you. I wanted you to exist here and be happy. Anyway, he says. I believe we have done a lot of good for each other. Yes. I know. It’s sad because it was the happiest time of her life, and it’s over now. Never again will she have what she had then, the love and care of another person. Never again will they be two plants sharing the same soil, one leaning in the light, the other languishing in the shade. She doesn’t blame him, she no longer believes her unhappiness is inevitable. No one can be what another person wants them to be. But she adds: You should go, if you want to. I’ll always be here. You know that. Does she think it’s possible to belong to someone this way? So concretely, so unquestionably. To have someone belong to you. The scene could still unite them, for those minutes, so that it would be unthinkable to be separated from him again, unthinkable that they had wasted so long already. But she knows he won’t be confused about what he has to do with his life. She knows he’ll go and she’ll stay, and that’s how it will be. People can really change one another. You should go, she says. I’ll always be here.

Yeah, said Marianne. It is. It’s a really big thing. I know. She wrapped her cardigan tighter around herself. It was cold in the room. Connell fidgeted. He sat on his hands and rocked back and forth, then said: It would be hard. Leaving all this. I won’t have the life that I have with you. It would be a half-life or something. She knew they would not be the same after they parted from each other, but that things would be all right. She looked out the window as big drops of rain came down, one after the other, flattening themselves against the glass. Connell wiped his nose on his sleeve. His eyes were pink. Marianne thought about it, what it would really be like. Connell would uproot out of the soil, their soil, and he would go somewhere new. And, while Marianne would miss him, and perhaps feel lonely, she would never feel unworthy again. She said, out loud: That’s something you can’t take away, isn't it? written_by_MFA013.Original: That was the only time, as I stood there, looking at that strange rubbish, feeling the wind coming across those empty fields, that I started to imagine just a little fantasy thing, because this was Norfolk after all, and it was only a couple of weeks since I’d lost him. I was thinking about the rubbish, the flapping plastic in the branches, the shore-line of odd stuff caught along the fencing, and I half-closed my eyes and imagined this was the spot where everything I'd ever lost since my childhood had washed up, and I was now standing here in front of it, and if I waited long enough, a tiny figure would appear on the horizon across the field, and gradually get larger until I'd see it was Tommy, and he'd wave, maybe even call. The fantasy never got beyond that --I didn't let it-- and though the tears rolled down my face, I wasn't sobbing or out of control. I just waited a bit, then turned back to the car, to drive off to wherever it was I was supposed to be.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt1: I was thinking about the rubbish, the flapping plastic in the branches, the shoreline of odd boots and bottled drinks along the banks of the little stream, and for a moment my thoughts segued to the people walking towards the Lost Corner, looking for all the world like they were out for a stroll. So I stopped and waited, the wind tugging with the odd gust through my hair, and just for the frustration of it all, of how my plans had been disrupted, I imagined that all the things I had lost in life had washed up here on this spot. In front of me, on the horizon, he came trudging towards me with that odd gait he had. He was waving and laughing, as if this was a little slice of fun, and I wanted to cry out "Tommy," but I didn't, and he came on, so happy and fun, and I could feel the tears welling up. But then I reeled it back, let the fantasy unwind, and just stood in my normal stance, blinking into the wind. When I felt ready, I got in the car and went on with my life.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: I stood in solitude in the grass field near the beach. Ten feet away, the grass gave way to sand, which then gave way to the ocean. The wind blew, scattering rubbish and abandoned belongings. An umbrella tumbled along the shoreline, and a plastic bag drifted past me. A wide variety of objects – presumably lost at sea or lost by patrons of the beach – washed up on the shore. I imagined that anything I’d lost throughout my life could be returned to me by those waves. Then I pictured Tommy approaching from the horizon, the hair on his legs wet and flat against his skin. I saw him wave at me, and was overcome by the pain of his absence. Tears welled in my eyes. I knew that he was not really there, Tommy had long since passed. Nevertheless, I found myself longing for him to come join me in the grass. I shut my eyes and stood still for a long moment. I dried my tears and became composed. I returned to my car, without looking back. Tommy was gone, I reminded myself. Life must go on.

written_by_MFA015.Original: That was the only time, as I stood there, looking at that strange rubbish, feeling the wind coming across those empty fields, that I started to imagine just a little fantasy thing, because this was Norfolk after all, and it was only a couple of weeks since I’d lost him. I was thinking about the rubbish, the flapping plastic in the branches, the shore-line of odd stuff caught along the fencing, and I half-closed my eyes and imagined this was the spot where everything I'd ever lost since my childhood had washed up, and I was now standing here in front of it, and if I waited long enough, a tiny figure would appear on the horizon across the field, and gradually get larger until I'd see it was Tommy, and he'd wave, maybe even call. The fantasy never got beyond that --I didn't let it-- and though the tears rolled down my face, I wasn't sobbing or out of control. I just waited a bit, then turned back to the car, to drive off to wherever it was I was supposed to be.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: There once existed a time here, I suppose, when I could walk this windswept field without knocking my feet against all that came before. But now the world has filled it up with itself. Children’s playthings that were surely once my own, kites wrapped around a wayward branch, brought here as if they’d always been. Because maybe they always had. It gets so I can see Tommy now, coming up over the hillside, waving at me the way he used to––as if I was all he wanted and could want out of this life. There was a morning much like this one, only as far back as a month ago. I’d seen him as himself then, with that same wave, that same wanting. But now he wasn’t anywhere, and it makes me ashamed to say I feel less of that darkness now than I did then, the day after we lost him. Tommy isn’t anywhere on the hillside. I stand only with the lesser wound and the tears that come despite it. I allow my feet to carry me back to the car, to head back into town for the night, with the hope that no one there knows my name.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: I was thinking about the rubbish, the flapping plastic in the branches, the shoreline of odd boots and bottled drinks along the banks of the little stream, and for a moment my thoughts segued to the people walking towards the Lost Corner, looking for all the world like they were out for a stroll. So I stopped and waited, the wind tugging with the odd gust through my hair, and just for the frustration of it all, of how my plans had been disrupted, I imagined that all the things I had lost in life had washed up here on this spot. In front of me, on the horizon, he came trudging towards me with that odd gait he had. He was waving and laughing, as if this was a little slice of fun, and I wanted to cry out "Tommy," but I didn't, and he came on, so happy and fun, and I could feel the tears welling up. But then I reeled it back, let the fantasy unwind, and just stood in my normal stance, blinking into the wind. When I felt ready, I got in the car and went on with my life.

The comparatively curt ending sentence then represents both a syntactic and emotional "come-down" or fall-off.

Excerpt 2 adds an extra couple breaks in its rendering, but overall maintains this breathlessness and nested sentence structure: "the rubbish, the flapping plastic in the branches, the shoreline of odd boots and bottled drinks...and for a moment my thoughts segued to the people...looking for all the world like they were out for a stroll." This stream-of-consciousness conveys a similar narrator interiority as the original. 

Excerpt 1 makes significant departures in approach and style from the original, although these departures are both evocative and effective. It breaks up its sentences and opts to spread the emotional climax into the ending sentence, past the initial moment with Tommy.

written_by_MFA011.Original: Then I called Reva. She answered on the fourth ring, panting and tense."I’m at the gym," she said. "Can we talk later?" We never did.On September 11, I went out and bought a new TV/VCR at Best Buy so I could record the news coverage of the planes crashing into the Twin Towers. Trevor was on a honeymoon in Barbados, I'd later learn, but Reva was lost. Reva was gone. I watched the videotape over and over to soothe myself that day. And I continue to watch it, usually on a lonely afternoon, or any other time I doubt that life is worth living, or when I need courage, or when I am bored. Each time I see the woman leap off the seventy-eighth floor of the North Tower—one high-heeled shoe slipping off and hovering up over her, the other stuck on her foot as though it were too small, her blouse untucked, hair flailing, limbs stiff as she plummets down, one arm raised, like a dive into a summer lake—I am overcome by awe, not because she looks like Reva, and I think it's her, almost exactly her, and not because Reva and I had been friends, or because I'll never see her again, but because she is beautiful. There she is, a human being, diving into the unknown, and she is wide awake.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: I’d spoken with Reva last week, but it was a short conversation filled mostly with platitudes. She’d seemed distracted and said she was at the gym. When the news broke about the towers, I called her a few times, but she didn’t pick up. Without thinking, I went immediately to the store to purchase a TV/VCR machine. Suddenly the most important thing was to record all the news footage that was blaring at me from out of my TV. I thought briefly about calling Trevor, then remembered that he was in Barbados on his honeymoon, probably sipping a drink with some spiky, inedible part of a fruit in it, completely unaware of what had happened. Once the sun went down and I still hadn’t heard from her, I realized that Reva was lost, likely for good. For days I sat watching and rewatching the footage I’d taped of the attacks, unable to move from in front of the TV save to piss or search the bathroom cabinet for more pills. There was a video of a woman leaping from the North Tower, and though it was too grainy for me to ever be able to tell if it was Reva, I liked imagining that it was.She wore a grey pencil skirt with black tights and stilettos – one still gripping her foot while the other had torn free, suspended in the air. She looked so beautiful, jumping like that into the unknown, that I took a kind of strange and holy comfort in her courage.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: "You should hang out more," I told Reva. "You'd like that, huh?" I could hear the whir of the machines in the background. "I gotta go, weirdo. I'm at the gym."On the morning of September 11, 2001, I went straight from the bodega where I got my coffee to Circuit City and charged a new TV/VCR combo on my Visa to record the news coverage. Trevor was on his honeymoon in Barbados. Everything was happening as it was supposed to. Reva was now "lost." For a full week I watched the same footage of the planes hitting the Twin Towers, the burning people plummeting, the buildings crumbling at the end like collapsing sand castles from every angle the news had to show.One woman leapt from a window from the North Tower and somehow caught my attention. She had on a skirt or a dress and was barefoot. As she spun, her stockings caught the updraft like sails, and I could see the outline of her thighs. She fell so gracefully. It looked almost like she was dancing. If I squinted, she looked like Reva. Of course I loved her—I had spent the last year mourning her as though she were dead. But I didn't cry. I wasn't hurt. I didn't feel sad. I just admired her, looked up at her there, so far above me and so elegant.

The original excerpt is anchored by the initial dialogue which frames the flux of the narrator's relationship with Reva when she dies, but also the minutiae of the city --- "TV/VCR at Best Buy...the seventy-eighth floor of the North Tower" and the lingering detail, both figurative and literal, on the woman's appearance and impression. In particular the minor details are crucial to understanding the narrator's detail-obsessed process of grieving. 

Excerpt 1 eschews specific details about the initial conversation ("short conversation filled with platitudes", electing instead to elaborate on Trevor's Honeymoon, and the narrator's compulsive inability to "move from the TV to piss or search the bathroom cabinet for piss." 

In contrast, Excerpt 2 maintains the original's focus on the two central components: the conversation with Reva, the little details of the city ("Circuit City...the bodega), and the sprawling description of the woman.

written_by_MFA008.Original: There was old sex in the room and loneliness, and expectation, of something without a shape or name. I remember that yearning, for something that was always about to happen and was never the same as the hands that were on us there and then, in the small of the back, or out back, in the parking lot, or in the television room with the sound turned down and only the pictures flickering over lifting flesh.We yearned for the future. How did we learn it, that talent for insatiability? It was in the air; and it was still in the air, an afterthought, as we tried to sleep, in the army cots that had been set up in rows, with spaces between so we could not talk. We had flannelette sheets, like children's, and army-issue blankets, old ones that still said U.S. We folded our clothes neatly and laid them on the stools at the ends of the beds. The lights were turned down but not out. Aunt Sara and Aunt Elizabeth patrolled; they had electric cattle prods slung on thongs from their leather belts.No guns though, even they could not be trusted with guns. Guns were for the guards, specially picked from the Angels. The guards weren't allowed inside the building except when called, and we weren't allowed out, except for our walks, twice daily, two by two around the football field, which was enclosed now by a chain-link fence topped with barbed wire. The Angels stood outside it with their backs to us. They were objects of fear to us, but of something else as well. If only they would look. If only we could talk to them. Something could be exchanged, we thought, some deal made, some tradeoff, we still had our bodies. That was our fantasy.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: We sit and watch Aunt Sara and Elizabeth as they walk slowly back and forth through the gymnasium, their skirts making the sound of waves as they scrape against the floor. We want to move, but we are afraid of the cattle prods, because we have seen what they do to others, the way bodies twist under them like writhing serpents, the way skin burns where the prods touched them for days after. We watch the Angels, too, guards who gaze into the distance as though they are somewhere else, far away. We imagine what it would be like to go to them, to touch their arms and their chests and their beards, to take off our clothes and show them our warm bodies, watch their faces unthaw at the sight of our soft and supple skin. We imagine a world where we beg for our freedom, for the chance to go outside, into the egg-colored sun, to step barefoot on the wet grass, to spin in the cool wind of the day. We imagine what it would be like to leave the cold, fetid horror of this place behind, let it become a memory, a vile, coppery taste at the backs of our throats. But we know better than to go to them. They are the ones with loaded guns, which they hold cradled in their arms like babies. We’ve seen what has happened to the girls who dare to speak to the Angels, the heaviness of a body when it falls to the floor after it’s been penetrated with a bullet, the deafening and definitive crack of the gunshot. For now, we sit and we watch. We stay still and we dream and we yearn. We wait and we imagine something other than the rigid darkness of today.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: The smell of the wood chips on the floors of the caged gymnasium where we slept, that stale, sweet odor; the moist sheen of bundled bodies, carried with us into the sunlight. I remember that yearning, that thirst for something we could never grasp. It wasn't just the touch of tongues and fingers, of sweaty thighs; it was a desire for the future. It was still in the air, an afterthought, as we tried to sleep. We created so many illusions for ourselves, of one kind or another. How else could we live? I remember whispering as we folded laundry late at night, those soft, slow voices moving through the humid air. We folded our clothes neatly and laid them on the stools at the end of the beds. In the semidarkness we could stretch out our arms, when the Aunts weren't looking, and touch each other's hands across space. We learned to lip-read, our heads flat on the beds, turned sideways, watching each other's mouths. In this way we exchanged names, from bed to bed: Alma. Janine. Dolores. Moira. June.The door was locked, and it was forbidden for us to be awake in here after lights-out. We were constantly being watched. Aunt Sara and Aunt Elizabeth patrolled; they had electric cattle prods worn on leather belts, but no guns. Guns were for guards, a.k.a. Angels. The guards weren't allowed inside the building except when they were bringing new women or taking the old ones away. They stayed outside, with their backs deliberately turned toward us. They were objects of fear, but familiarity dulled our apprehension. What we fantasized about more than anything else was the possibility of touching them, or having them touch us, using our bodies as the currency, the ultimate coin of exchange—what we would give them for freedom. There was nothing we wouldn't give.

written_by_MFA004.Excerpt2: Even their names were duplicitous, Aunt Sara and Elizabeth. Aunt Sara evoked the image of a mousy-haired woman who hoarded loose buttons and bright thread in a cookie tin. They carried cattle prods and the first time I’d seen one, gripped in Elizabeth’s wide hand, I’d sniffed the compound for a mealy smell of animals but was met with fecund whiffs of soil and the tart odor of women under stress. Holly, Rozalyn, and I were middle-age with new wrinkles yet cloistered and monitored like boarding school miscreants. We had a box of a room with pocked floors and standard bunk-beds, blue sheets that reminded of a hospital and not the sky. And where was the fourth girl, smart-mouthed Sara? She’d talked back at gender studies that morning, suggesting a definition of women that was beyond the womb. Sara had too much ambition and ambition was what the cattle prods corrected. Outside our picture-book sized window was a big square of yellow grass and men with guns who called themselves Angels. My favorite guard had a roman nose and thick, tan neck. I imagined that if I got close enough, I could lave my tongue, cat-like, up his neck. I was convinced he’d love me just from this, from those few seconds of wet, lancing heat. He’d take me in his arms and run me to freedom. At twilight, he liked to shoot at the crows in the sky. With that rain of holy fire escaping his gun, he looked blessed and impossible to crucify, an angel indeed.

written_by_MFA005.Original: "The only reason you say that race was not an issue is because you wish it was not. We all wish it was not. But it’s a lie. I came from a country where race was not an issue; I did not think of myself as black and I only became black when I came to America. When you are black in America and you fall in love with a white person, race doesn’t matter when you’re alone together because it’s just you and your love. But the minute you step outside, race matters. But we don’t talk about it. We don’t even tell our white partners the small things that piss us off and the things we wish they understood better, because we’re worried they will say we’re overreacting, or we’re being too sensitive. And we don’t want them to say, Look how far we’ve come, just forty years ago it would have been illegal for us to even be a couple blah blah blah, because you know what we’re thinking when they say that? We’re thinking why the fuck should it ever have been illegal anyway? But we don’t say any of this stuff. We let it pile up inside our heads and when we come to nice liberal dinners like this, we say that race doesn’t matter because that’s what we’re supposed to say, to keep our nice liberal friends comfortable. It’s true. I speak from experience." The host, a Frenchwoman, glanced at her American husband, a slyly pleased smile on her face; the most unforgettable dinner parties happened when guests said unexpected, and potentially offensive, things.The poet shook her head and said to the host, “I’d love to take some of that wonderful dip home if you have any left,” and looked at the others as though she could not believe they were actually listening to Ifemelu. But they were, all of them hushed, their eyes on Ifemelu as though she was about to give up a salacious secret that would both titillate and implicate them. Ifemelu had been drinking too much white wine; from time to time she had a swimming sensation in her head, and she would later send apology e-mails to the host and the poet. But everyone was watching her, even Blaine, whose expression she could not, for once, read clearly. And so she began to talk about Curt.
written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: "Race doesn't really exist for you because it has never been a barrier. Black folks don't have that choice. Like, growing up in Nigeria, I knew I was black, but I didn't really think about it until I came to America. Then I came here and—God, it hits you immediately. Race becomes everything. You can't say in good faith race doesn't matter when you are dating a white man. The minute you step outside, things are apparent. When somebody walks into a bar that you are sitting in with your white husband, they don't see a man and a woman; they see a white man and a black woman. It doesn't matter what they say. At the grocery store, they'll ask you, separately, if you need help, because, of course, it's such a stretch to imagine that you're together. written_by_MFA012.Original: I breathed in the night air that was or was not laced with anachronistic blossoms and felt the small thrill I always felt to a lesser or greater degree when I looked at Manhattan’s skyline and the innumerable illuminated windows and the liquid sapphire and ruby of trafﬁc on the FDR Drive and the present absence of the towers. It was a thrill that only built space produced in me, never the natural world, and only when there was an incommensurability of scale—the human dimension of the windows tiny from such distance combining but not dissolving into the larger architecture of the skyline that was the expression, the material signature, of a collective person who didn’t yet exist, a still-uninhabited second person plural to whom all the arts, even in their most intimate registers, were nevertheless addressed. Only an urban experience of the sublime was available to me because only then was the greatness beyond calculation the intuition of community. Bundled debt, trace amounts of antidepressants in the municipal water, the vast arterial network of trafﬁc, changing weather patterns of increasing severity— whenever I looked at lower Manhattan from Whitman’s side of the river I resolved to become one of the artists who momentarily made bad forms of collectivity ﬁgures of its possibility, a proprioceptive ﬂicker in advance of the communal body. What I felt when I tried to take in the skyline—and instead was taken in by it—was a fullness indistinguishable from being emptied, my personality dissolving into a personhood so abstract that every atom belonging to me as good belonged to Noor, the ﬁction of the world rearranging itself around her. If there had been a way to say it without it sounding like presumptuous co-op nonsense, I would have wanted to tell her that discovering you are not identical with yourself even in the most disturbing and painful way still contains the glimmer, however refracted, of the world to come, where everything is the same but a little different because the past will be citable in all of its moments, including those that from our present present happened but never occurred. You might have seen me sitting there on the bench that midnight, my hair matted down from the bandanna, eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, and having, as I projected myself into the future, a mild lacrimal event.
written_by_MFA012.Excerpt1: I breathed in the night air that might or might not have smelled like blossoms. Looking at the incomparable skyline of Manhattan, I felt a familiar thrill - one I'd never been able to explain, though I knew it came from seeing those tiny illuminated windows set against the massive forms that contained them.The thrill was so intense and singular that it must have been more than just the visual relationship, for apart from a cityscape, nothing natural or man-made held my attention long enough to provoke it. What I saw, I thought, was a material form of the second person plural, the true subject of art. It was sublime, a plural subject, skyline as collective body coming into being, a body that didn't exist yet, something to which you could belong in the future and sometimes in the present tense. It only appeared solid, towering, but all the things that produced the sublime effects were bad: titanic banks bundling debt against the general welfare, measurable traces of antidepressants in the water supply, traffic networks poisoning the air, and ever-worsening storms. I'd long felt that one wanted to be an artist to make bad forms of collectivity appear as the promise of an almost unimaginable good: not reified abstraction, poorly disguised negation of the one in the many, but the emerging collective that would do justice to the wrongs absorbed by the bodies below the skyline. Tonight the fiction of the world—all my strongest perceptions, including rare fictions of participation in a benevolent collectivity—had gathered around Noor as if she were a black hole. Through her I was being changed more fully into a thing, a person among persons, and the experience was only horrible to the extent that it wasn't total. The uncanny feeling of not being identical with yourself, of being a stranger to your own experience, is profoundly alienating, yet it holds a glimmer of utopian hope. This sense of dislocation is available to be felt as a rearticulation, a promise that the past can be unlocked in the present. It is the paradoxical hope that in the moment you realize you are not yourself, you experience the possibility of becoming another, allowing the past to be reconfigured, rewritten in the now.I thought all this at midnight on a cheap folding bench with my hair flattened by a bandanna, eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, tearing up a little—a mild lacrimal event—projecting myself into this scene from the future.
written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: Gazing upon the skyline of Manhattan, I inhaled the stench of the sewers, the smoke of the gyro stand, and the fragrance of blossoms. For me, steel landscapes always followed this progression: first coarseness, then delectability, then something more subtly appetizing. The longer I looked, the more thrilling the tableau revealed itself to be, with the yellowed hued windows forming a jagged arcade. The buildings were so immense that I didn’t think of mountains so much as other buildings, particularly the skyscrapers-in-progress I had recently encountered in an architecture magazine. Granite ranges—not to mention waterfalls, alluvial plains, verdant valleys, desert mesas, and the like—have seldom made an impression on me. Yet this skyline, being the result of over a century of steel-hewn collective striving, provoked a deeper recognition; in the risings and falls of the rooftops, I pinpointed a material beyond that which the builders had worked with—something all-encompassing, a “you” to which a work of art would surely be addressed. Perhaps every work of art in the history of humankind—from the verses of Sappho, to the triumphs of Muslim architecture, to brush strokes of the Dutch masters, to the Goldberg Variations—had been addressed to this “you.” All the bundled debt of midtown was merely a muse to a Greek woman’s pen; pigments intermingled in the city water supply with the traces of antidepressants; the gridlock on the Brooklyn Bridge recalled the stylings of Ibn Tulun. Did the fog setting in over the river contain a hint of Bach? I couldn’t quite tell. Yet it didn’t matter: the world was a sprawling racket of collaboration, full of bad forms of collectivity which, as an artist, I could transform into something more, a brighter “you.” Of course, at that moment, as I meditated on the skyline, Noor insinuated herself into my thoughts. It was only natural, considering how the fiction of the world swarmed around her. As I sat on the bench, I almost felt as if I was sitting upon Noor, upon “you.” My consciousness waned into another—and was this such a crime? One could not be identical with oneself—but could one be better? After reaffixing my bandana to my head, and consuming an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, I found myself suffering a mild lacrimal event. Would the world make a skyline within you? Would we ever be a part of the human tangle?

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: I inhale the night, which has the faint taste of blossoms hanging on it. I always found it thrilling to watch the city this way, how the illuminated windows on apartment buildings and offices cling together as parts of an expansive and profoundly intricate skyline. The beauty others find in a mountain, a valley, a crested hill, I find in looking at urban mosaics like these, like Manhattan, this grand forest of buildings and bridges and smoke and air. I find that nature feels too much like a singular entity, a crystalline cohesion, whereas urban landscapes feel like a second person plural, something that does not exist now, but exists only in the future, a future where everything, art and intimacy and joy and expansion, has room to breathe and move. It’s almost unbearable, the sublimity of the bundled debt, the anti-depressants that stream through urine and into the water supply, the light pollution, traffic in the sky and on the ground, all connecting to create something artful and strange and united. This is what I think of when I gaze at the skyline, how I will become an artist, one who transforms and reshapes bad modes of collectivity into the possibility for good, into a broad future where all entities can exist in the same body. I think of Noor—how can I not?— and my connection to her, her connection to us all, her large and shapeless body, which the fiction of the world organizes itself so perfectly around. I am alone. I am alienated. And I am the alienator—I have no false pretenses about this. How ironic it feels, sometimes, to know that I am alone, and yet not even identical with myself. Is it foolish that I find some hope in that? That I think of Noor and I feel her and I smell the blossoms of the city night and I understand that the past and present are formless, shapeless, and can be reorganized, reimagined into something bigger? I sit here and I look at the skylight. It’s midnight, and I am on a bench that’s cold and, I think, slightly damp, though it’s hard to tell. My eyes are blurry with exhaustion, my hair flattened by that blue bandanna from Goodwill, and I am eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango from a Ziplock bag. My eyes begin to burn, a mild lacrimal event, as I think of all this possibility. My fingertips are slightly slippery, sugared from the fruit I’m eating.
