written_by_MFA016.Original: One evening ‒ it was our last day ‒ in Tours, we had dinner in a brightly-lit restaurant where the walls were lined with mirrors, frequented by a sophisticated clientele. My father and I were seated at the end of a long table set up for the group. The waiters were paying little attention to us; we had to wait a long time between courses. At a small table nearby sat a girl aged fourteen or fifteen, suntanned, in a low-cut dress, and an elderly man who appeared to be her father.They were talking and laughing quite freely, completely at ease, oblivious of other people. She was dipping into a thick milky substance in a glass ‒ some years later I learnt this was yogurt, which people like us had never heard of. I caught sight of myself in the mirror, pale and sad-looking with my spectacles, silently sitting beside my father, who was staring into the far distance. I could see everything that separated me from that girl yet I wouldn’t have known what to do to resemble her.Afterward, my father complained with unusual vehemence about this restaurant, where he claimed we had been served mashed potatoes made with “pig slop,” white and tasteless. Several weeks later, he was still venting his anger over the meal and its disgraceful “pig slop.” Although he never actually said so ‒ it was probably then that I began decoding his speech ‒ it was his way of expressing resentment at having been treated with contempt because we were not chic customers who ate “à la carte.”
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: We sat there, my father and I, at the group table. Anyone looking our way could see our discomfort. I touched my spectacles and watched myself in the great wall mirror - each time finding myself paler and more repulsive. My father grew more agitated, too, letting our meager conversation drop, because the waiter had still not come with his mashed potatoes after so many dreary minutes. I watched a girl near my age across the room dining at her own special table with an older man. I watched her through the mirror in case she might meet my eye. She was tan and lifted a spoon of creamy yogurt to her lips. I was lost, for a moment, in imagining its flavor. I had never tasted yogurt before. When our food came at last, it looked nothing like the pretty plate in front of the tan girl - the same way my clothes looked nothing like hers - the same way my skin matched the grey sky outside while hers glowed like the sun in the tropics. Later, in the streets and at home, my father repeatedly talked about the "pig slop" they served him at the restaurant and vowed never to return. It took me years to understand how he was complaining - in his own way - of the hurt that came with seeing, but never ordering, "à la carte."
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: The restaurant was an annex to the Trois-Couronnes.I had a pale face and was wearing my spectacles that day, which made me look sad. That wasn't the issue, though. My father and I had been seated at the table reserved for groups, on the far side of the dining room, and were ignored throughout the meal. At the next table, there was a man with his daughter, who was older than I was, maybe seventeen, sleek and tanned with short blonde hair. I remember a long, gilt-framed mirror hanging above their heads, reflecting endless repetitions of identical people. The girl talked confidently to her father and laughingly spooned up her yogurt. In those days, I didn't know what yogurt was. She seemed at home, oblivious to her surroundings, wearing no jacket or headscarf, simply her checkered summer dress. She made me feel awkward and ashamed, although I couldn't explain why, my only desire being to leave as soon as possible. Later on, walking along the streets, my father kept saying, "Those mashed potatoes looked like pig slop." For the first time, I realized that he had been marking time to continue, repeating the reason why he hadn't eaten anything on his plate. I didn't think of asking him what difference it made what the potatoes looked like. Deep down, he was upset at being treated as a second-class customer just because we weren't dining "à la carte" like the people sitting near us.

written_by_MFA013.Original: “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine. Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine. Please contact the pharmacy immediately.” The announcement played again, but Dr. Y was apparently still missing.The elevator was crowded with doctors and nurses, and patients with drip bags of yellow liquid, but I forced my way in and pressed the button for the sixth floor. I was sure I’d be able to find her room. I would pretend I was just visiting her, or I could say I wanted her to pay me for the bag. After all, I ought to get something for all my work.First, I’ll apologize for the other day—very humbly, in order to regain her trust. And then I’ll say what I’ve come to say: “Making your bag has been a very important experience for me. I don’t think I’ll ever have the chance to make a piece like this again. Still, I’m happy you’re getting the operation and won’t need the bag. But I do have one final request: I’d like to see it put to its intended use just once. I know it’s asking a lot, but I’d be very grateful. I promise I’ll never bother you again, but nothing is more painful for a craftsman than knowing all his hard work was for nothing. Just this once, and I’d be eternally grateful.”She’ll take off her gown, and I’ll fit it on her.“Are you satisfied, then?” she’ll ask, eager to be rid of me.“Thank you,” I’ll say, but when I reach for the bag, I’ll cut her heart away, too.And then it will be mine alone.The bag is in my left pocket. I tried to fold it flat, but there’s a little mound in my pants. I don’t think anyone will notice. The shears in my right pocket prick my thigh as I wait.The elevator chimes, the number six lights up, and the door opens.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt1: The elevator doors opened. It was crowded, so I pushed my way inside. Doctors and nurses stood shoulder to shoulder in one corner. I joined the patients and visitors that grouped in another. The doors closed, and the elevator began its ascent. The tightly packed bodies offset the hospital's sterile smell. I had been told that I would find Rin on the sixth floor. I clutched the bag I brought for her, made heavy by the shears within. I wondered if she'd notice the care I put into making her bag the same way I noticed the care with which she used to tend her shrubs. Before her accident, she'd rise early to trim them, and I could see her from the window of my workshop. Watching her felt almost voyeuristic at first. The precision with which she used her shears excited me, reminiscent of the delicate way I stitched my handbags. We rarely spoke, but perhaps watching her in this way made me envy her. I had seen her work, but she had never seen mine. I planned to present her with the bag, one of the best I'd constructed, as a gesture of good will in hope of regaining her trust. I would politely request she accept the bag, and see if she admired it the way I admired her shrubs. Then I would remove the shears. I imagined that revealing them to her, while she was in such a helpless state from her injuries, would cause alarm. After all, I could easily plunge them into her, trim around her chest like one of her shrubs, and cut away her heart. She'd be helpless to stop me, and I could claim the bag I made for her alone. "Attention: Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine, telephone please. Dr. Y, telephone please," a voice over a speaker said. The elevator stopped at last, and I arrived on the sixth floor.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: I was on my way to see the woman as a visitor, riding up in an elevator filled with doctors and nurses clutching clipboards, and patients doubled over in pain. "Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine is needed in the consulting room," an announcement came over the PA system. Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine, however, never showed his face.My purpose in visiting her was clear enough: I intended to meet with her, regain her trust, and convince her to let me see the bag put to its intended use one last time."Would you mind undoing the ends of the cord so I can check how you attached it?" "Would you like me to take a photograph of you wearing it?" "Do you need to have another hole punched in the strap to make it longer?" I rehearsed these lines in my head. I realized I had never spoken to her so politely.In truth, I simply needed to make her put the bag down for a moment. I planned to face her, extend to her all the gratitude I felt for having been allowed to sew the bag on. Then, once she let her guard down, I would press the shears to her chest. The shears were hidden, but soon she'd feel the cold steel pressed against her belly, slowly moving up toward her breasts. She'd moan in fear. I'd then carefully—oh so carefully—slice through the flesh as though cutting through layers of delicate silk. When the final thread had been cut and the heart was liberated from her chest, there would be no need anymore to smile and exchange pleasantries. The bag would be mine alone. But not because I wanted it. No, I was doing this to restore the proper order of things. I'd hold the bag in one hand and the shears in the other. The elevator finally climbed to the sixth floor.
written_by_MFA013.Reason: E2 is more similar to the Original than P1. The digression into the past that we see in E1 about the shrubs feels wrong in terms of the style of the Original. written_by_MFA015.Original: On my last visit, my father seemed in worse condition than I had seen him before. When I asked him if he was working on anything in particular now, he said no and then turned his head slowly to my mother and looked at her in bewilderment, his mouth hanging open. There was an expression of pain or agony on his face that seemed habitual. She looked back at him, waited a moment, impassive, and then said: “Yes, you are. You’re writing about the Bible and anti-Semitism.” He continued to stare at her. Later that evening, before he went to bed, he said: “This is symptomatic of my condition: You’re my daughter, and I’m proud of you, but I have nothing to say to you.” He left to get ready for bed, and then came back into the room wearing dazzling white pajamas. My mother asked me to admire his pajamas, and he stood quietly while I did. Then he said: “I don’t know what I will be like in the morning.” After he went to bed, my mother showed me a picture of him forty years before sitting at a seminar table surrounded by students. “Just look at him there!” she said in distress, as though it were some sort of punishment that he had become what he was now—an old man with a beaked profile like a nutcracker.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: I had gone there and didn’t know what to do after I’d gone there. At my father’s house, I entered his study where he sat at his desk staring at his hands. Next to his hands, his work––book stacks on biblical theology and anti-Semitism. I stood behind him. I stared at his hands. This was a turning point of sorts of ours, his hands, our staring at them. So many hours of ours went to this, had come to this. I thought: when did we get here? And: what do I do now, now that we’ve gone here? My mother came in and laid her own hand on his shoulder. She said, “Gerry” which was my father’s name, “Gerry, remember, you were working on your essay on biblical theology and anti-Semitism.” She made a sweeping motion with her hands before him. When he finally saw me, he said, “My daughter…” and told me how proud he was of me and all that I’d been doing. Then he said he had nothing else to say to me. He went back to his hands. Later that evening, my mother and I sat in the dining room together, where she showed me an old photograph of my father. “What happened to him?” my mother said, and I couldn’t tell her. I couldn’t even come close to saying.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: When I came to the house and saw his face, I understood that his condition had worsened. He had a look of fear and incomprehension. He sat in a straight-backed chair, torpid with his medication. The lining was coming out of his jacket on both sides, into his lap. He had been forgetting where he put his papers, then losing them, too, and forgetting what he was working on. Mother would remind him: he was working on a long book about the Bible and anti-Semitism. His memory would be jogged, he would go on working until he forgot again. Father told me that day: “I am proud to have a daughter like you.” Then he added that he had nothing to say to me, nothing at all. He said, “It’s because we have isolated ourselves.” He fell silent and turned away from me. “We have isolated ourselves.” That was all. There was nothing I could say. That evening, Mother showed me a photograph taken forty years before, when my father had just got his degree: he had large brown eyes and a full head of silver hair that stood up above his head. “I can’t stand this,” she said quietly. “It is intolerable. He is such a different person.”

In terms of style, E2 also feels more successful in that its descriptors focus on small, striking details, much like the Original (O: "Dazzling white pajamas" E2: "The lining was coming out of his jacket on both sides...").

written_by_MFA027.Original: On my last visit, my father seemed in worse condition than I had seen him before. When I asked him if he was working on anything in particular now, he said no and then turned his head slowly to my mother and looked at her in bewilderment, his mouth hanging open. There was an expression of pain or agony on his face that seemed habitual. She looked back at him, waited a moment, impassive, and then said: “Yes, you are. You’re writing about the Bible and anti-Semitism.” He continued to stare at her. Later that evening, before he went to bed, he said: “This is symptomatic of my condition: You’re my daughter, and I’m proud of you, but I have nothing to say to you.” He left to get ready for bed, and then came back into the room wearing dazzling white pajamas. My mother asked me to admire his pajamas, and he stood quietly while I did. Then he said: “I don’t know what I will be like in the morning.” After he went to bed, my mother showed me a picture of him forty years before sitting at a seminar table surrounded by students. “Just look at him there!” she said in distress, as though it were some sort of punishment that he had become what he was now—an old man with a beaked profile like a nutcracker.
written_by_MFA027.Excerpt1: When I came to the house and saw his face, I understood that his condition had worsened. He had a look of fear and incomprehension. He sat in a straight-backed chair, torpid with his medication. The lining was coming out of his jacket on both sides, into his lap. He had been forgetting where he put his papers, then losing them, too, and forgetting what he was working on. Mother would remind him: he was working on a long book about the Bible and anti-Semitism. His memory would be jogged, he would go on working until he forgot again. Father told me that day: “I am proud to have a daughter like you.” Then he added that he had nothing to say to me, nothing at all. He said, “It’s because we have isolated ourselves.” He fell silent and turned away from me. “We have isolated ourselves.” That was all. There was nothing I could say. That evening, Mother showed me a photograph taken forty years before, when my father had just got his degree: he had large brown eyes and a full head of silver hair that stood up above his head. “I can’t stand this,” she said quietly. “It is intolerable. written_by_MFA027.Excerpt2: I barely recognized my father when I entered the kitchen, which was probably because he completely failed to recognize me. All my life I had felt only he knew my name. written_by_MFA007.Original: Before the flight I was invited for lunch at a London club with a billionaire I’d been promised had liberal credentials. He talked in his open-necked shirt about the new software he was developing, that could help organisations identify the employees most likely to rob and betray them in the future. We were meant to be discussing a literary magazine he was thinking of starting up: unfortunately I had to leave before we arrived at that subject. He insisted on paying for a taxi to the airport, which was useful since I was late and had a heavy suitcase.The billionaire had been keen to give me the outline of his life story, which had begun unprepossessingly and ended – obviously – with him being the relaxed, well-heeled man who sat across the table from me today. I wondered whether in fact what he wanted now was to be a writer, with the literary magazine as his entrée. A lot of people want to be writers: there was no reason to think you couldn’t buy your way into it. This man had bought himself in, and out, of a great many things. He mentioned a scheme he was working on, to eradicate lawyers from people’s personal lives. He was also developing a blueprint for a floating wind farm big enough to accommodate the entire community of people needed to service and run it: the gigantic platform could be located far out to sea, thus removing the unsightly turbines from the stretch of coast where he was hoping to pilot the proposal and where, incidentally, he owned a house. On Sundays he played drums in a rock band, just for fun. He was expecting his eleventh child, which wasn’t as bad as it sounded when you considered that he and his wife had once adopted quadruplets from Guatemala. I was finding it difficult to assimilate everything I was being told. The waitresses kept bringing more things, oysters, relishes, special wines. He was easily distracted, like a child with too many Christmas presents. But when he put me in the taxi he said, enjoy yourself in Athens, though I didn’t remember telling him that was where I was going.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: A billionaire once invited me to lunch at his club in London. It was a grand place, but the billionaire wore skinny jeans, a hooded top, and designer trainers without a care in the world. He was very keen to show me his latest software project, which was a program that could predict which employees in a company would next betray their boss. I had to catch a plane immediately afterwards and so was a little restless, and he insisted on paying for my taxi to the airport, which was nice, since I'd come with a suitcase. We were supposed to be talking about a literary magazine he wanted to start, and I hadn't expected his personal security software to come up. But when we sat down and started, it was he who told me the story of his life. I assembled the biography: a humble beginning, the lessons in work and intellect, and finally this  tawny-haired and surprisingly well-muscled figure at the table across from me. I guess he imagined that the literary magazine might provide some sort of entrée into the practice of writing, seeing as he'd got and done pretty much everything else with his money. He told me a lot more – about the complexity and immensity of his entrepreneurial schemes, such as a floating wind farm that would house and provide credit for its workers and thereby solve the problem of world poverty and ecocide; or another scheme he had for legally disposing of lawyers from people's personal lives. He also mentioned that he'd taken up playing drums in a rock band every Thursday night, because why not; and that he was presently expecting his eleventh child, counting the Guatemalan quadruplets he and his wife had adopted earlier. The billionaire talked for so long that I couldn’t keep up with it all, I was almost too exhausted to follow. Waitresses kept arriving, removing dishes and bringing huge plates of lobster and bottles of fine wine. His focus was so scattered, his enthusiasm so limitless, it was almost like that of a child. Enjoy yourself in Athens, he said, putting me in the taxi afterwards, though I didn't remember mentioning I was going there.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: Before I left the country, a billionaire invited me to lunch at a London club. I’m working on a software for HR operations, he said. He wore an outfit that defied the club’s dress code: a dark T-shirt and darker jeans. It uses a predictive algorithm, he said, that scrapes employee backgrounds, e-mails, and market trends to identify which ones are likeliest to betray their companies. But I’ve been getting carried away. I’m starting a literary magazine; let’s discuss it. Unfortunately, by the time the literary subject came up, I’d already finished my entree and needed to leave for the airport. He insisted on paying for my taxi, which I accepted. I was late for my flight and carried a heavy suitcase. The billionaire had spent most of our lunch sharing his life story, which began with him as a humble public-school student and ended with him becoming the wealthy man leaning back in the chair across from me. I figured he wanted to use the literary magazine as a launchpad to becoming a writer himself. It wouldn’t be a ridiculous notion—he bought his way into a number of things. He told me he’d built a floating wind farm, located offshore from the township he was designing to house its workers. He also said he had a scheme to eliminate lawyers from people’s everyday lives and personal problems. For fun, he played drums in a psychedelic rock band, though he wasn’t writing any original songs. He was expecting his eleventh child, a surprise pregnancy; he and his wife had recently adopted quadruplets from Guatemala. Throughout the lunch, I found it difficult to respond thoughtfully, or even adequately, to the billionaire’s many ventures and projects. The waitresses kept bringing in appetizers on porcelain plates—foie gras, baked brie, oysters—and drinks in crystal glasses—mimosas, champagne. The billionaire jumped from topic to topic, and when his voice rose an octave as he described eliminating inefficiencies, he reminded me of a child barreling through the halls of an opulent mansion. At the end of lunch, he put me in the taxi and said, Enjoy yourself in Athens. I didn’t remember telling him where I was going?
written_by_MFA007.Reason: E1is more similar in voice and style to the Original than E2. I think the main issue with E2 is the voice. It has a bit more of a breezy, casual affect than the Original's voice, which feels more erudite yet unadorned and a bit judgemental (O: "A lot of people want to be writers: there was no reason to think you couldn’t buy your way into it.". E2 feels almost like it's addressing the reader (E2: "I didn't remember telling him where I was going?"). E2 also feels like it includes too much detail, and includes direct dialogue that feels at odds with the Original narrator's very insular style of storytelling. P1, in contrast, maintains this insular style and removed tone (P1: "I guess he imagined that the literary magazine might provide some sort of entrée into the practice of writing, seeing as he'd got and done pretty much everything else with his money."), even if (in my opinion) it might be less colorful/interesting to read than the Original and E2.

written_by_MFA030.Original: "There are no words. The one I send home comes out a pukka Englishman, white suited, silly wig lawyer. But if you believe that, where do you go? What do you do? What does anything matter?"

I'll get that swapped out for you right away.""He didn't even think to argue. Part of me wants him to tell me to go back to whatever 'istan' I'm from. 'Sir,' he calls me, 'sir.' Like part of me has rotted to be like the forever rotten core of them and they smell it too. But isn't that what I always wanted? Isn't that why I came to this country? I swear these warring sides of myself must have migrated to my reproductive organs, for just look at my children," said Samad bitterly."I think of the children. Varush, he just sticks out that stiff upper lip all day and god, that accent—sometimes I just want to unhook his jaw and stuff it full of chai, and tell him to go back where we came from. But then Malik, the other boy, always complaining that everything is offensive and everyone is oppressing us. These children, I swear, sometimes I just want to walk away from them.""Oh, that's not true, surely," Irie says."Please do not underestimate the ability of a father to forsake his children! If I was a man before I made the devil's pact and came here, I am something less now.". The waiter is taking long. Samad drinks the tea and the ash all in one gulp. "I want to feel all of its worlds inside me. But really, they just vanish, like they never existed at all", he says.
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2:
"Well, life's dealt some rather unkind cards. One son, a pukka Englishman—a suit-wearing, diploma-carrying, Tory-voting coward—while my other son has gone from muttering one-liners about infidels to a bloody fundamentalist terrorist. I can't say it surprises me. Yes, I made a devil's pact; yes, yes—but please tell me where was the better option? My father, from whom I could never escape, made quite sure there was only one road to be taken. To hell with it. This is the suffering of the immigrant: of my generation and Archibald's, immigrants by necessity, English by residence but not by birth. For us first-generation folk, those who came here fleeing hardship, there is always the struggle to make a home, a real home, in what remains another's land."

For so many of us, it is far too late to go back. Better to give up the very idea of belonging. I truly tried to give my children roots and culture and language and traditions, but all I have succeeded in giving them is the sickness of the immigrant, the curse of the stuck-in-between. But at the same time, I can't forget what I lost. Balance, my friend. Balance."

written_by_MFA029.Original: The news about Walter Berglund wasn’t picked up locally—he and Patty had moved away to Washington two years earlier and meant nothing to St. Paul now—but the urban gentry of Ramsey Hill were not so loyal to their city as not to read the New York Times. According to a long and very unflattering story in the Times, Walter had made quite a mess of his professional life out there in the nation’s capital. His old neighbors had some difficulty reconciling the quotes about him in the Times (“arrogant,” “high-handed,” “ethically compromised”) with the generous, smiling, red-faced 3M employee they remembered pedaling his commuter bicycle up Summit Avenue in February snow; it seemed strange that Walter, who was greener than Greenpeace and whose own roots were rural, should be in trouble now for conniving with the coal industry and mistreating country people. Then again, there had always been something not quite right about the Berglunds.Walter and Patty were the young pioneers of Ramsey Hill—the first college grads to buy a house on Barrier Street since the old heart of St.Paul had fallen on hard times three decades earlier. They paid nothing for their Victorian and then killed themselves for ten years renovating it. Early on, some very determined person torched their garage and twice broke into their car before they got the garage rebuilt. Sunburned bikers descended on the vacant lot across the alley to drink Schlitz and grill knockwurst and rev engines at small hours until Patty went outside in sweatclothes and said, “Hey, you guys, you know what?” Patty frightened nobody, but she’d been a standout athlete in high school and college and possessed a jock sort of fearlessness. From her first day in the neighborhood, she was helplessly conspicuous. Tall, ponytailed, absurdly young, pushing a stroller past stripped cars and broken beer bottles and barfed-upon old snow, she might have been carrying all the hours of her day in the string bags that hung from her stroller. Behind her you could see the baby-encumbered preparations for a morning of baby-encumbered errands; ahead of her, an afternoon of public radio, the Silver Palate Cookbook, cloth diapers, drywall compound, and latex paint; and then Goodnight Moon, then zinfandel.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: It must have been easier, in the late stages, not to have the story spilling directly into local news outlets. Easier to keep up the front. The Times erred only once, as far as one can tell, and described Walter as "arrogant" and "ethically compromised." Yet this dissonant portrait would not have resonated locally anyway, since Walter and Patty had already moved to Washington, D.C., about two years earlier. He'd gone to work for some energy-conservation organization after his youngest left college. It was hard to reconcile the full story with the optimistic, rural, green Walter who appeared to have been hampered and then corrupted by city life. Nowhere was the irony more poignant than back in St. Paul. The memory of the simple Walter, committed to punishing bad neighbors and raising good kids, stood in contrast to the fall of a man now willing to cut deals with big coal companies and ethically bend the rules in pursuit of his goals.To understand the derailment of Walter and Patty Berglund, one must remember those early years in Ramsey Hill when they were young pioneers in a neighborhood struggling to reclaim its nineteenth-century grandeur. The Berglunds bought their big Victorian for a song in 1990, when nobody wanted those properties because of broken windows, stray gunshots, and derelict urbanites holding out in rotting pillboxes. written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: The people of St. Paul did not know what to make of the article; no, they could not even begin to wrap their heads around it. If they squinted, they could all picture Patty outside, painting over the word "Fuck" that a hooligan had sprayed onto the house's flank one night: she with her unflinching athleticism, the kind acquired in college sports, pushing a stroller with that well-weathered batting arm, a bag of apples in the other. If she was not standing on a ladder, scraping out the gutters like a man, she was drinking zinfandel at that gorgeous kitchen island she'd done herself, the public radio on, too loudly for most of the other women's tastes. The couple would throw dinner parties and put signs up in their yards about the ocean and sometimes fight so loudly that the people down the hill had to shut their windows to protect them, in their kind Midwestern way, from the shame of having been heard.

written_by_MFA029.Original: We started dying before the snow, and, like the snow, we continued to fall. We were surprised that so many of us were left to die. For those who survived the spotted sickness from the south and our long fight west to Dakota land, where we signed the treaty, and then a wind from the east, bringing exile in a storm of government papers, what descended from the north in 1914 seemed terrible, and unjust.By then we thought disaster must surely have spent its force, that disease must have claimed all of the Anishinabe that the earth could hold and bury.But along with the first bitter punishments of early winter a new sickness swept down. The consumption, it was called by young Father Damien, who came in that year to replace the priest who had succumbed to the same devastation as his flock. This disease was different from the pox and fever, for it came on slowly. The outcome, however, was just as certain. Whole families of Anishinabe lay ill and helpless in its breath. On the reservation, where we were forced close together, the clans dwindled. Our tribe unraveled like a coarse rope, frayed at either end as the old and new among us were taken. My own family was wiped out one by one. I was the only Nanapush who lived. And after, although I had seen no more than fifty winters, I was considered an old man.I guided the last buffalo hunt. I will not sign—we will not be exiles again. Too much has already been taken. The Anishinabe persist, and I will continue to resist for the Pillagers who are lost, and for those of us who carry on.

written_by_MFA007.Original: We started dying before the snow, and, like the snow, we continued to fall. We were surprised that so many of us were left to die. written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: Before my life, the Anishinabe were traveling people. We had been on the move for generations. First we went in quest of food, and then in search of land to call home. written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: First, in the south, we were stormed by the spotted sickness, little red bumps that went from the blanket to the body; then, by the gun, we moved westward to Dakota land, thousands of us dragging our feet across endless miles. Those of us who didn't drop dead from the spots signed a treaty. Before long, we moved once more, condemned to exile, our land taken away by right of the government's stamped document. 1914: Another sickness called 'consumption' rolled in as a terrible storm does, its invisible winds running into our mouths and choking us. After all that, we coughed to our deaths. It came slowly: not like a massacre but like a lost war. We were living six to a room back then, and the cough jumped from one Anishinabe brother to another. The whole Pillager family became ill within a fortnight, the eight of them wasting away in a single room. My whole family went, too. Our tribe, once a tightly woven quilt, unraveled; the knots came loose, the patterns disintegrated into bright threads. Merely fifty years have passed since my birth, yet I am now called an elder, the last of the Nanapush. I remember the end of our lives, the final rites of our traditions. I led the last buffalo hunt. I saw the last bear shot. I trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt. I felled the last birch tree older than a sapling. I remember how, as the sickness razed our people, I went into the room with the eight members of the Pillager family. I fed them water, buffalo meat, and bread. I brought them wet cloths and herbs to ease their fever and coughing. I saved the last of them, the daughter. And I remember receiving the government papers that would rid us of our land and rights. I refused to sign.

written_by_MFA025.Original: Valentine farm is a delusion. Who told you the negro deserved a place of refuge? Who told you that you had that right? Every minute of your life’s suffering has argued otherwise. By every fact of history, it can’t exist. This place must be a delusion, too. Yet here we are.And America, too, is a delusion, the grandest one of all. The white race believes—believes with all its heart—that it is their right to take the land. To kill Indians. Make war. Enslave their brothers. This nation shouldn’t exist, if there is any justice in the world, for its foundations are murder, theft, and cruelty. Yet here we are.“I’m supposed to answer Mingo’s call for gradual progress, for closing our doors to those in need. I’m supposed to answer those who think this place is too close to the grievous influence of slavery, and that we should move west. I don’t have an answer for you. I don’t know what we should do. The word we. In some ways, the only thing we have in common is the color of our skin. Our ancestors came from all over the African continent. It’s quite large. Brother Valentine has the maps of the world in his splendid library, you can look for yourself. They had different ways of subsistence, different customs, spoke a hundred different languages. And that great mixture was brought to America in the holds of slave ships. To the north, the south. Their sons and daughters picked tobacco, cultivated cotton, worked on the largest estates and smallest farms. We are craftsmen and midwives and preachers and peddlers. Black hands built the White House, the seat of our nation’s government. The word we. We are not one people but many different people. How can one person speak for this great, beautiful race—which is not one race but many, with a million desires and hopes and wishes for ourselves and our children?
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Valentine Farm is what you get when a bunch of world-weary people dream of sanctuary. Like a dream, this collective delusion is gone by morning light. It’s fake, a lie. Though if a place can be a haven, I wonder if Black Americans deserve the refuge more than anyone else. Certainly, after everything this country has stolen, we deserve something in return. But then I suspect that if there is a sanctuary to be found, Black Americans probably built it, just like they built the rest of this country. I fear it’s impossible to find any semblance of peace inside a façade you were forced to build. And no façade is greater than America. America is the grandest delusion of them all, built on pillars of murder, theft, and cruelty. A cruelty that runs so deep in white Americans that it inspires entitlement, a fundamental belief that the land and lives of others is of no consequence to them, so why not take it? Justice can’t breathe in a place like this. America’s very existence contradicts the concept of right and wrong. What then, is the right thing to do? Do we stay here, and chip away at progress, do we close our doors to those in need, or do we throw it all away to run west, hoping to start anew in a place slavery never touched? Maybe we’ll find buried gold, get rich, and erect a thousand new Valentine Farms. I just don’t know. And who is “we” anyways? Black Americans are no monolith. Africa saw thousands of languages, customs, and histories. The only thing that makes us a “we” is slavery. Even in slavery, there was no uniformity. Craftsmen, midwives, laborers—laborers who built the White House! There is no “we.” Too many voices are clamoring to be heard, crying their many dreams and experiences and fears. No one voice will be able to speak for all these dreams.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm is a delusion. Who among us slaves and freedmen, free-born and fugitives, believes they are due that rare circumstance of happiness? We can escape slavery on paper, but not in real life. The verdict of history is clear: no small paradise like Valentine can smoothly elude it. And America is the grandest delusion of them all, founded on murder, theft, and cruelty. Its architects built castles and keeps while never dealing fairly with Indians or ourselves, venerating a religion which they hollow out with their practiced cruelties.You scratch below the surface and find the blood, everywhere. The white race believes everything belongs to them. The slave state of Georgia is as much theirs as the free state of Massachusetts. They believe they can wage war, put their neighbors in chains, and appropriate the heavens and the earth. One delusion however remains: justice. What to do now? Wait? Welcome everyone who comes to our door or move west to the edge of the continent to escape the shadow of slavery? I have no answers. Who is to say what is right? And when I say 'we,' who am I talking about? In some ways, the only thing we have in common is the color of our skin. Our ancestors came from all over the African continent. Different tribes, languages, and traditions made the trip across the ocean, landing on the same shores to be sold on the same auction block. We're not a single people. We're root and branch, leaf and vine, toiling, insensible to each other's qualities and flourishing. Brick by brick, we built this nation: the roads, the canals, the factories, and even the White House. We tilled the fields under the whip for King Cotton, and over their silks and finery, they proclaimed their nobility. We are craftsmen and craftswomen, more than a race of midwives and howling babies, bishops and preachers and dissembling lackeys. No one voice can speak for us all.
written_by_MFA025.Reason: The original excerpt is delivered as a speech, and as such, it's written in a direct style, without metaphorical flourishes or highly formal language: "Brother Valentine has the maps of the world in his splendid library, you can look for yourself. They had different ways of subsistence, different customs, spoke a hundred different languages." The first excerpt, however, relies more heavily on metaphors, and elaborate flourishes more appropriate for written language (rather than spoken): "Valentine Farm is what you get when a bunch of world-weary people dream of sanctuary. Like a dream, this collective delusion is gone by morning light." The second excerpt, while often using formal language, does not employ these visual metaphors to the same extent; instead, it directly refers to historical events, the suffering under slavery: "Our ancestors came from all over the African continent. Different tribes, languages, and traditions made the trip across the ocean, landing on the same shores to be sold on the same auction block." While the first excerpt often relies on rhetorical flourishes ("Justice can’t breathe in a place like this" or "Too many voices are clamoring to be heard, crying their many dreams and experiences and fears. No one voice will be able to speak for all these dreams"), the second excerpt refers directly to the lived experience of enslaved Black Americans: "We tilled the fields under the whip for King Cotton, and over their silks and finery, they proclaimed their nobility." We are craftsmen and midwives and preachers and peddlers. Black hands built the White House, the seat of our nation’s government."

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: I thought Valentine Farm was a delusion, a dream-land. There was a real question in my mind as to whether a place like it ought to even exist for Black people. Too much blood was on American ground and in it for such a place to exist. The only thing more fake was America - I thought America was the grandest delusion of all. White men had slaughtered Native Americans and taken the land for themselves, enslaving Black folks to work on it. They warred with each other, forcing us to fight in their battles. There was something fundamentally wrongheaded about the idea that there could be a place of safety and refuge amidst all of that violence and suffering, past and present. And I wondered if there was any point in hoping that things would get better. I wasn't sure of it, and I thought that maybe it would be best to just close Valentine Farm's doors altogether. Or - head West, try to escape the past by moving into the future. Forget all that suffering, all that blood. We needed to do something, but I didn't know what. I didn't even know who "we" was, really. They liked to tell us we were all the same, but I knew better. Back in Africa, we were thousands of different tribes, each with our own language, our own dances, our own gods. We could tell each other apart, and then we crossed an ocean and suddenly we were all Black. We were all Black, and we were told to work, and we waded through the blood fresh on the earth to build this whole country. The roads, the cities. The White House. All of us with our hands, each one calloused and worn in its own unique way, each one different. All of us Black, and all of us our own people, with our own wants and desires, impossible to condense into just one solitary thing.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: Valentine Farm is a delusion. It's no more real than one of those heat shimmers that disappear as you step closer. How could Black people even have a haven like that? The transatlantic ships, the endless days of toiling, the many nights of dying—they already preclude the possibility of a sanctuary. It's too late. It's impossible. The scars can't heal—they're white, carved on our cheeks. And America itself is the grandest delusion, a series of territories thrown together on the basis of mass murder, theft, and cruelty. The white race believes it has the right to do all this—the right to take land, start wars, enslave us. The very existence of America defies the notion of justice. Now, I suppose there are two possibilities left. We can pursue gradual progress: reform, speech-making—and close our doors to those in need. Or we can move west, to someplace far from the violent grasp of slavery, to somewhere fresher and less polluted. I don't have an answer. I can't even say who "we" are. Aren't "we" many peoples, descended from all over the vast continent of Africa? It may not be the case anymore, but generations ago, "we" spoke different languages. "We" worshiped different gods. "We" had different kings, farmed different vegetables, sang different songs with different instruments. There is only one thing that unites us: slavery. Here, now, in this foreign land, we are craftsmen, midwives, laborers. We are everything to this violent country. It was Black people who quarried the stone of the White House, who assembled its roof and walls. And we are not a monolith. Each of us holds a singular amount of courage, of ambition, of love. Each of us has suffered in unique ways. Each of us sees something different when we look into the eyes of our children. There is no single voice that can speak for us. Not even mine.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm is a delusion. Who among us slaves and freedmen, free-born and fugitives, believes they are due that rare circumstance of happiness? We can escape slavery on paper, but not in real life. The verdict of history is clear: no small paradise like Valentine can smoothly elude it. And America is the grandest delusion of them all, founded on murder, theft, and cruelty. Its architects built castles and keeps while never dealing fairly with Indians or ourselves, venerating a religion which they hollow out with their practiced cruelties.You scratch below the surface and find the blood, everywhere. The white race believes everything belongs to them. The slave state of Georgia is as much theirs as the free state of Massachusetts. They believe they can wage war, put their neighbors in chains, and appropriate the heavens and the earth. One delusion however remains: justice. What to do now? Wait? Welcome everyone who comes to our door or move west to the edge of the continent to escape the shadow of slavery? I have no answers. Who is to say what is right? And when I say 'we,' who am I talking about? In some ways, the only thing we have in common is the color of our skin. Our ancestors came from all over the African continent. Different tribes, languages, and traditions made the trip across the ocean, landing on the same shores to be sold on the same auction block. We're not a single people. We're root and branch, leaf and vine, toiling, insensible to each other's qualities and flourishing. Brick by brick, we built this nation: the roads, the canals, the factories, and even the White House. We tilled the fields under the whip for King Cotton, and over their silks and finery, they proclaimed their nobility. written_by_MFA009.Original: To crave and to have are as like as a thing and its shadow. For when does a berry break upon the tongue as sweetly as when one longs to taste it, and when is the taste refracted into so many hues and savors of ripeness and earth, and when do our senses know any thing so utterly as when we lack it? And here again is a foreshadowing—the world will be made whole. For to wish for a hand on one’s hair is all but to feel it. So whatever we may lose, very craving gives it back to us again. Though we dream and hardly know it, longing, like an angel, fosters us, smooths our hair, and brings us wild strawberries.Sylvie was gone. She had left without a word, or a sound. I thought she must be teasing, perhaps watching me from the woods. I pretended not to know I was alone. I could see why Sylvie thought children might come here. Any child who saw once how the gleaming water spilled to the tips of branches, and rounded and dropped and pocked the softening shadows of frost at the foot of each tree, would come to see it again.If there had been snow I would have made a statue, a woman to stand along the path, among the trees. The children would have come close, to look at her. Lot’s wife was salt and barren, because she was full of loss and mourning, and looked back. But here rare flowers would gleam in her hair, and on her breast, and in her hands, and there would be children all around her, to love and marvel at her for her beauty, and to laugh at her extravagant adornments, as if they had set the flowers in her hair and thrown down all the flowers at her feet, and they would forgive her, eagerly and lavishly, for turning away, though she never asked to be forgiven. Though her hands were ice and did not touch them, she would be more than mother to them, she so calm, so still, and they such wild and orphan things.
written_by_MFA009.Excerpt1: Sometimes I wonder about the difference between craving something and fulfillment. Sometimes I want something so much I feel like I’m going to break open. Let’s say it’s a fresh berry, let’s say it’s like I’ve been really wanting a fresh berry, plucked from a bush in the orchard, even before that berry’s in my hands, it’s already got a taste in my mind, I’ve been building it up moment after moment until I have it in my brain like I’ve already got it on my tongue, so when Sylvie tells me she picked something for me and plops it in my mouth, it’s even sweeter because the sweetness confirms the foundation I’ve already built for it. I don’t know how to put it. Sylvie disappeared for a while, like a mouse, but then she came back. Sometimes she still goes out though, vanishes into the woods without saying anything. I think she’s out there right now, watching me ruminate. I don’t know what kind of solitude we can both get when we both are in each other’s minds. Could it be a way of being together? A very strange way? It’s beautiful out in the woods. The trees are older than I can fathom, really, old like stories can be old. I’d like to put a status out there, almost like somebody would always be watching, a statue of a woman, to stand in between all those old trees, a woman in a crown of new flowers, looking only ever ahead, forward, never letting any kind of barrenness touch her, like she was the opposite of Lot’s wife and all there was to her was the kind of forgiving vibrancy that children wonder at, the vibrancy that comes from a life well-lived. Even as a statue, I think they’d come to her, every child that’s ever felt lost-wild and orphan, and I think when they’d reach out to touch her stone hands, they’d find that that statue’s stone was warm for them. Sometimes I wish Sylvie were warmer. There’s warmth all around in all the beautiful trees and even the grasses. The problem is that trees don’t feel warm when you touch their bark unless it’s from the sun.
written_by_MFA009.Excerpt2: Craving and its indulgence are really one and the same thing. There might be no fruits, and still, if one wished for them, yearned for them, one would taste them all. The very sight of a berry in the wild is an admonishment not to pick it, for when it is stored in the vision and played upon by desire, the taste it bears is gifted to it as much by memory as by its savor. The flavor grows until it is too exquisite for the tongue, unencumbered by flesh. So it is when one wishes for a friend, or a woman, or a child. For Sylvie disappeared and made no sound, and I fancied when I had closed my eyes and rocked awhile that she was not gone. It was easier than I could have imagined to pretend I was not alone, to insist that she merely watched me from the woods. The wind was dying, the sun was sinking, the side of the house was cooling, the evening moths were glancing and settling, and her absence was a thing so full of longing it became a presence of its own. If I could row the lake at dawn and gather all the proud blossoms from the woods for one year, I would throw some across the graves of unsanctified and dreamless children and some into the holes of fox dens. And with the rest I would sculpt from snow a statue of a woman. I would stand her in the clearing in the woods, and she would be adorned with rare flowers with leaves like hands, with hardstem thistles, and the birds would rest in her. Lot's wife would have none of this: flowers in profusion and children. Her breast caved into a hollow of regret. Not this one, not my mother. All the wild children, who knew too well that the world does not give itself generously to children, would burst from the trees and behold her. And every child, the most orphaned, the most bereft, would forgive her for her frozen hands and would stand at her white hem in awe that she should seem to shower them with blossoms, eternally offering what she could never give, inexplicably so stern.
written_by_MFA009.Reason: The first excerpt is much too conversational; there is a confessional tone to it ("Sometimes I wonder about ...), moments of first-person self-doubt ("I don't know how to put it), a simplicity to its vocabulary ("Let’s say it’s a fresh berry, let’s say it’s like I’ve been really wanting a fresh berry"), and run-on sentences. The original excerpt, however, maintains a poetic and philosophical tone; while it is also in first-person, its narrator is confident, almost objective, in her descriptions, so that it sounds closer to exposition than conversation: "To crave and to have are as like as a thing and its shadow. For when does a berry break upon the tongue as sweetly as when one longs to taste it, and when is the taste refracted into so many hues and savors of ripeness and earth, and when do our senses know any thing so utterly as when we lack it?" The second excerpt comes much closer to that "objective," philosophical voice: "Craving and its indulgence are really one and the same thing. There might be no fruits, and still, if one wished for them, yearned for them, one would taste them all." The use of "one" in that sentence, for example, rather than positioning it as an "I"-statement, allows the sentence to feel philosophical/objective rather than a personal meditation.

And here again is a foreshadowing—the world will be made whole. For to wish for a hand on one’s hair is all but to feel it. So whatever we may lose, very craving gives it back to us again. Though we dream and hardly know it, longing, like an angel, fosters us, smooths our hair, and brings us wild strawberries.Sylvie was gone. She had left without a word, or a sound. I thought she must be teasing, perhaps watching me from the woods. I pretended not to know I was alone. I could see why Sylvie thought children might come here. Any child who saw once how the gleaming water spilled to the tips of branches, and rounded and dropped and pocked the softening shadows of frost at the foot of each tree, would come to see it again.If there had been snow I would have made a statue, a woman to stand along the path, among the trees. The children would have come close, to look at her. Lot’s wife was salt and barren, because she was full of loss and mourning, and looked back. But here rare flowers would gleam in her hair, and on her breast, and in her hands, and there would be children all around her, to love and marvel at her for her beauty, and to laugh at her extravagant adornments, as if they had set the flowers in her hair and thrown down all the flowers at her feet, and they would forgive her, eagerly and lavishly, for turning away, though she never asked to be forgiven. Though her hands were ice and did not touch them, she would be more than mother to them, she so calm, so still, and they such wild and orphan things.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: Craving and its indulgence are really one and the same thing. There might be no fruits, and still, if one wished for them, yearned for them, one would taste them all. The very sight of a berry in the wild is an admonishment not to pick it, for when it is stored in the vision and played upon by desire, the taste it bears is gifted to it as much by memory as by its savor. The flavor grows until it is too exquisite for the tongue, unencumbered by flesh. So it is when one wishes for a friend, or a woman, or a child. For Sylvie disappeared and made no sound, and I fancied when I had closed my eyes and rocked awhile that she was not gone. It was easier than I could have imagined to pretend I was not alone, to insist that she merely watched me from the woods. The wind was dying, the sun was sinking, the side of the house was cooling, the evening moths were glancing and settling, and her absence was a thing so full of longing it became a presence of its own. If I could row the lake at dawn and gather all the proud blossoms from the woods for one year, I would throw some across the graves of unsanctified and dreamless children and some into the holes of fox dens. And with the rest I would sculpt from snow a statue of a woman. I would stand her in the clearing in the woods, and she would be adorned with rare flowers with leaves like hands, with hardstem thistles, and the birds would rest in her. Lot's wife would have none of this: flowers in profusion and children. Her breast caved into a hollow of regret. Not this one, not my mother. All the wild children, who knew too well that the world does not give itself generously to children, would burst from the trees and behold her. And every child, the most orphaned, the most bereft, would forgive her for her frozen hands and would stand at her white hem in awe that she should seem to shower them with blossoms, eternally offering what she could never give, inexplicably so stern.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: I’ve realized that craving and fulfillment are not connected in the way I once thought. A craving is so intense and visceral that it cannot be truly satiated by consuming the thing you want. For example, berries are always sweeter before I eat them. I wonder if that’s how Eve felt in the garden after she tasted the forbidden fruit—disappointed, hungry, running her tongue over her teeth in search of satisfaction. I’ve been thinking about Sylvie, and how she disappeared silently into the forest and left me alone. I suspected she might be hiding somewhere, watching from a perch atop a spruce tree or huddled inside a hollow log. She liked to tease me. I didn’t want to give her the satisfaction of calling out for her, making her think I was afraid of being alone. I didn’t want her to feel like she’d rescued me by returning. I meandered around the little clearing and looked at the great towering tree trunks and their long shadows and the patches of grass poking up from the dark earth. In the center of it all, I imagined a statue. She was carved from some kind of pale, luminescent stone, something that seemed to give off its own light from within. Rare flowers were twined in her hair—orchid doves, lenten roses, midnight clematis. Blossoming vines wound up her body, not trapping her, but protecting her. My statue was a radiant mother, utterly unlike the barren, remorseful wife of Lot. She was vibrant and forgiving, always surrounded by children who marveled at her quiet beauty. The children, wild vagabonds of the forest, would be drawn to her through some mysterious summons, and they would huddle before her and bask in her gentle solace. Though her frozen hands would never touch them, she would look upon them with a kindness they had never known, and their happy tears would feed the vines and flowers that had made her their home. When the children were with her, they were not orphans, but children who had been made to be loved by a mother.
written_by_MFA029.Reason: Excerpt 1 is closer to the original because it preserves the length, movement and the abstractions that lead the reader to the subject, as the original does. Excerpt 2, on the other hand, starts sentences with a declaration of thought and fact, through phrases like "I've realized" and "for example," "I've been thinking" and "I didn't want." The original, on the other hand, doesn't project so much onto Sylvie, and only uses phrases like "I thought she must be teasing," or "I pretended not to know" to obfuscate than to clarify. Similarly, Excerpt 1 uses "I would" to talk about hypothetical or possible situations than to make something clear. Although the diction of Excerpt 1 is slightly more elevated, it doesn't hinder the poetic nature of the original. Furthermore, in Excerpt 2, the narrator says "my statue" rather than the narrator making a statue, as described in the original and Excerpt 1.

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: There are times when to long for something is almost as satisfying as to finally receive it, or when the essence of that which is desired is evoked so clearly that to receive it is no longer necessary. As when one yearns to pluck a berry from the vine and savor its ripeness, so that the sweetness seems to precede the taste of the juice itself. Sylvie had said earlier that in springtime we could pick berries here. I searched for Sylvie's hand beside mine, but I found that she had slipped away silently and left me alone in the clearing. Yet in some way, I felt I could sense her closeness and thought she might be watching me from the woods, so I showed no change in my expression and pretended to be ignorant of my solitude. Around me, the sun cast long shadows through the partings of the tree branches, from which the browned leaves had already begun to fall into the clearing. A thin layer of frost was formed on the mud around where I sat. I imagined forming out of this cold clay earth a statue of a woman whom I would adorn with rare flowers. She would be a calm presence standing among the trees, not the cold, hard pillar of salt into which Lot's wife was transformed as punishment for her desire, for turning back with regret to look at all she had lost. A figure free of yearning, around whom the wild children of the forest would gather to marvel at her beauty and warmth. They would take solace in the vivacious beauty of such a figure and cling to her almost as a mother, even as her frozen hands could not caress them as one would their own children. Again I looked for Sylvie and thought of how I was, in searching for someone who had left me, not unlike the poor woman who had been turned to salt. Unlike the taste of those imagined berries, I was not sure if my longing for connection could ever be quite enough to evoke the presence of the thing itself.

For when does a berry break upon the tongue as sweetly as when one longs to taste it, and when is the taste refracted into so many hues and savors of ripeness and earth, and when do our senses know any thing so utterly as when we lack it? And here again is a foreshadowing—the world will be made whole. For to wish for a hand on one’s hair is all but to feel it. So whatever we may lose, very craving gives it back to us again. Though we dream and hardly know it, longing, like an angel, fosters us, smooths our hair, and brings us wild strawberries.Sylvie was gone. She had left without a word, or a sound. I thought she must be teasing, perhaps watching me from the woods. I pretended not to know I was alone. I could see why Sylvie thought children might come here. Any child who saw once how the gleaming water spilled to the tips of branches, and rounded and dropped and pocked the softening shadows of frost at the foot of each tree, would come to see it again.If there had been snow I would have made a statue, a woman to stand along the path, among the trees. The children would have come close, to look at her. Lot’s wife was salt and barren, because she was full of loss and mourning, and looked back. But here rare flowers would gleam in her hair, and on her breast, and in her hands, and there would be children all around her, to love and marvel at her for her beauty, and to laugh at her extravagant adornments, as if they had set the flowers in her hair and thrown down all the flowers at her feet, and they would forgive her, eagerly and lavishly, for turning away, though she never asked to be forgiven. Though her hands were ice and did not touch them, she would be more than mother to them, she so calm, so still, and they such wild and orphan things.
written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: There are times when to long for something is almost as satisfying as to finally receive it, or when the essence of that which is desired is evoked so clearly that to receive it is no longer necessary. As when one yearns to pluck a berry from the vine and savor its ripeness, so that the sweetness seems to precede the taste of the juice itself. Sylvie had said earlier that in springtime we could pick berries here. I searched for Sylvie's hand beside mine, but I found that she had slipped away silently and left me alone in the clearing. Yet in some way, I felt I could sense her closeness and thought she might be watching me from the woods, so I showed no change in my expression and pretended to be ignorant of my solitude. Around me, the sun cast long shadows through the partings of the tree branches, from which the browned leaves had already begun to fall into the clearing. A thin layer of frost was formed on the mud around where I sat. I imagined forming out of this cold clay earth a statue of a woman whom I would adorn with rare flowers. She would be a calm presence standing among the trees, not the cold, hard pillar of salt into which Lot's wife was transformed as punishment for her desire, for turning back with regret to look at all she had lost. A figure free of yearning, around whom the wild children of the forest would gather to marvel at her beauty and warmth. They would take solace in the vivacious beauty of such a figure and cling to her almost as a mother, even as her frozen hands could not caress them as one would their own children. Again I looked for Sylvie and thought of how I was, in searching for someone who had left me, not unlike the poor woman who had been turned to salt. Unlike the taste of those imagined berries, I was not sure if my longing for connection could ever be quite enough to evoke the presence of the thing itself.
written_by_MFA005.Excerpt2: Craving and its indulgence are really one and the same thing. There might be no fruits, and still, if one wished for them, yearned for them, one would taste them all. The very sight of a berry in the wild is an admonishment not to pick it, for when it is stored in the vision and played upon by desire, the taste it bears is gifted to it as much by memory as by its savor. The flavor grows until it is too exquisite for the tongue, unencumbered by flesh. So it is when one wishes for a friend, or a woman, or a child. For Sylvie disappeared and made no sound, and I fancied when I had closed my eyes and rocked awhile that she was not gone. It was easier than I could have imagined to pretend I was not alone, to insist that she merely watched me from the woods. The wind was dying, the sun was sinking, the side of the house was cooling, the evening moths were glancing and settling, and her absence was a thing so full of longing it became a presence of its own. If I could row the lake at dawn and gather all the proud blossoms from the woods for one year, I would throw some across the graves of unsanctified and dreamless children and some into the holes of fox dens. And with the rest I would sculpt from snow a statue of a woman. I would stand her in the clearing in the woods, and she would be adorned with rare flowers with leaves like hands, with hardstem thistles, and the birds would rest in her. Lot's wife would have none of this: flowers in profusion and children. Her breast caved into a hollow of regret. Not this one, not my mother. All the wild children, who knew too well that the world does not give itself generously to children, would burst from the trees and behold her. And every child, the most orphaned, the most bereft, would forgive her for her frozen hands and would stand at her white hem in awe that she should seem to shower them with blossoms, eternally offering what she could never give, inexplicably so stern.

written_by_MFA012.Original: “Try this one,” said Jack, “and I’ll say it just one time. Tell you what, we could a had a good life together, a fuckin real good life. You wouldn’t do it, Ennis, so what we got now is Brokeback Mountain. Everything built on that. It’s all we got, boy, fuckin all, so I hope you know that if you don’t never know the rest. Count the damn few times we been together in twenty years. Measure the fuckin short leash you keep me on, then ask me about Mexico and then tell me you’ll kill me for needin it and not hardly never gettin it. You got no fuckin idea how bad it gets. I’m not you. I can’t make it on a couple a high-altitude fucks once or twice a year. You’re too much for me, Ennis, you son of a whoreson bitch. I wish I knew how to quit you.”Like vast clouds of steam from thermal springs in winter the years of things unsaid and now unsayable—admissions, declarations, shames, guilts, fears—rose around them. Ennis stood as if heart-shot, face grey and deep-lined, grimacing, eyes screwed shut, fists clenched, legs caving, hit the ground on his knees.“Jesus,” said Jack. “Ennis?” But before he was out of the truck, trying to guess if it was heart attack or the overflow of an incendiary rage, Ennis was back on his feet and somehow, as a coat hanger is straightened to open a locked car and then bent again to its original shape, they torqued things almost to where they had been, for what they’d said was no news. Nothing ended, nothing begun, nothing resolved.
written_by_MFA012.Excerpt1: “You the storm that stranded me here,” said Jack. “Ain’t no other way to put it. I been thinkin on it, bustin my brain to try and fit the bits together, but it’s bullshit. You know it is, Ennis, don’t pretend like you don’t. I’ve called you, sent you letters first class, and you actin like the offseason applies to us. Brokeback’s just a little vacation, a couple ranch-hands in heat. Maybe you like it like that. You sure got me on a short leash. That’s all I am to you, Ennis: a bitch for the summer. I’d swallow glass if it meant I could spend the rest a my life on Brokeback, but you won’t even pick up the goddam phone.” Jack looked at the ridgeline. “I wish I knew how to quit you.” Ennis got down on one knee, and for a second Jack thought he was tying his shoe. Sobs wracked his ribs. “Jesus!” yelled Jack. Ennis kept crying. He looked down at the earth, the denim of his knee stirring up dust. To Jack he looked like a wounded horse, its hooves at rest. He feared for Ennis, this man for whom he had stored up so much love and hate. A cold distant man making a scene on the roadside—it didn’t make much in the way of sense. Jack had more to say but his jaw stayed shut. Ennis sobbed. After awhile he went still. Ennis pulled himself to his feet and pushed the dust off his jeans. Jack looked at him and Ennis looked back, but there was nothing there. Just the clouds of steam rising.
written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: Jack said what he said every time: "I'm tellin' you this one time, and I ain't foolin'. What I want—know why we're here? I want to know why, if I'm up in Lightning Flat in December and you're down in Texas maybe come June, why the hell can't I meet you somewhere in between for a few days? Hell, count them few times we been together in the same damn place. I got a gutful of it, enough. I'm done bein' dumb about this, see? When the hell we gonna get a chance to get it right? We been a fuckin' pair! And you know damn well what I'm sayin'. Damn you, Ennis del Mar. Brokeback Mountain—we kill ourselves up there. That's all we've got. Damn you. You've got me on a short leash, hung me up for years. Sometimes I miss you so much I can hardly stand it. I wish I knew how to quit you." Tears were running down Jack's face.Like vast, powerful haymakers, these words were blows that knocked a man down without warning. Ennis sagged to his knees seeking  to catch his breath. "Jesus," said Jack, thinking the man was having a heart attack as he knelt beside Ennis on the poured slab, putting his arm around his shoulder. Once the shock had passed Ennis hauled himself to his feet, flinched away from Jack, turned his back to him, and tried to be calm. He lit a cigarette, unbuckled his belt, and pulled his shirt out of his jeans. Nothing changed except who they were and what they felt—a silence that rose between them like clouds of steam.

Notice that these are mostly grammatically incorrect and charged, making it easier to grasp Jack's voice and frustration as language strains under the emotion.

Out there, you ain’t anybody I ever known. All we got here are moments on Brokeback Mountain, and moments ain’t a life, ain’t close to living. How much more of ourselves are you willing to let die? Don’t you know how much less of me I feel of myself? You keep all that I am on the shortest leash, Ennis. You are the one keeping us from the fullness of what our lives could be. Maybe you can keep on like this, but I can’t. I’m at the end of that rope. God, Ennis. I want to quit you. I wish I knew how to quit you.” Nearing the tailend of these words Ennis’s knees buckled, his body softened, as if having taken birdshot to his backside, though to Jack any outer wound could not be found. Jack went silent then, and kept it, unsure what to do with Ennis screaming, “Jesus, Jesus…” And though Ennis calmed, and the air on the mountain steadied, nothing had changed. Still they would go on as they had before, no one in the world knowing what they had between them, except them. The pain on that mountain would go on with them, too, would follow them into the days and weeks ahead, so weighty, like clouds of steam rising between the two.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: Jack said what he said every time: "I'm tellin' you this one time, and I ain't foolin'. What I want—know why we're here? I want to know why, if I'm up in Lightning Flat in December and you're down in Texas maybe come June, why the hell can't I meet you somewhere in between for a few days? Hell, count them few times we been together in the same damn place. I got a gutful of it, enough. I'm done bein' dumb about this, see? When the hell we gonna get a chance to get it right? We been a fuckin' pair! And you know damn well what I'm sayin'. Damn you, Ennis del Mar. Brokeback Mountain—we kill ourselves up there. That's all we've got. Damn you. You've got me on a short leash, hung me up for years. Sometimes I miss you so much I can hardly stand it. I wish I knew how to quit you." Tears were running down Jack's face.Like vast, powerful haymakers, these words were blows that knocked a man down without warning. Ennis sagged to his knees seeking  to catch his breath. "Jesus," said Jack, thinking the man was having a heart attack as he knelt beside Ennis on the poured slab, putting his arm around his shoulder. Once the shock had passed Ennis hauled himself to his feet, flinched away from Jack, turned his back to him, and tried to be calm. He lit a cigarette, unbuckled his belt, and pulled his shirt out of his jeans. Nothing changed except who they were and what they felt—a silence that rose between them like clouds of steam.
written_by_MFA015.Reason:
The dialogue in the original excerpt feels almost too private for the reader to hear or access. Excerpt 1 does a better job of preserving that sense of ambiguity, rupture and extreme intimacy. The speech unfolds in a similarly breathless style, and lines such as “How much more of ourselves are you willing to let die?”—feel desperate and raw. Excerpt 1 also matches the original’s apocalyptic tone. The moment where Ennis’s body is seen collapsing—“as if having taken birdshot to his backside”—echoes the original’s image of his legs caving in, crumpling to the ground.

Excerpt 2, by contrast, feels overly scripted and direct. Lines such as “Sometimes I miss you so much I can hardly stand it” over-explain the situation. In addition, the naming of places, such as “Lightning Flat” or "Texas" makes the voice feel more grounded and reportorial than it is in the original.

Nothing ended, nothing begun, nothing resolved.

written_by_MFA006.Excerpt1: “Thing is,” Jack said, “I’m fucking sick of it. Tired of goin nowhere but up the mountain with you. Givin me just Brokeback Mountain is bout as good as givin me nothin, and you know it. I want more–I want it all–and I don’t reckon you’ll ever give it to me. I’m like your dog, chokin on your short leash. All I want is to…it doesn’t matter, do it? Imma dog frothin at the end of your fuckin leash. Goddammit.” He paused for a moment, his breath coming out in short, steaming pants that warmed the tent. “Goddammit. I wish I knew how to quit you.”Jack’s words acted like a rusted arrow upon Ennis–tired, worn out, but not without their raw edge, dangerously sharp. They pierced through him, brought him down to his knees. He lay there on the ground, clutching himself, pale, his wide-eyed gaze fixed on the mountain. “Jesus–” Jack stooped down as if to help him. Was he sick? Jack wondered. Was he finally able to see? Jack’s hands hovered around the other man’s body, but Ennis looked so far away, as if dreaming, and impossible to touch. Ennis got up without his help, recomposing his face into that flat, familiar expression. He rose up from his knees, a man rewound–the dramatic act reversed, so that again he became just a man with a lockbox of feelings. Just Ennis, slumped against the valley. That same far off expression on his face, his hand, gently trembling, grasping at nothing. And that same pain was there too, a shared pain–hot, palpable, unresolved and unrelenting–like clouds of steam rising between them.
